‭rates to be approved that allow for the development of required capital‬
‭upgrades and a guaranteed return on equity.‬

‭Q. Why does Central Hudson have a drive to expand its rate base?‬
‭A.‬‭In rate cases, PSC-regulated utilities are guaranteed‬‭a return on equity,‬
‭which is a metric for profit as a percentage of their rate base. The rate base is a‬
‭utility's approved capital investments minus depreciation. Thus, the size of the‬
‭rate base is a critical driver of the amount of profit a utility can expect to earn,‬
‭and there is a motive for utilities to invest in expensive approvable capital‬

‭Q. What is the conflict between Central Hudson’s obligation to provide‬
‭just and reasonable rates and its drive to expand its rate base?‬
‭A.‬ ‭For investor-owned utilities, there is such a‬‭thing as smart financial‬
‭investment even if it does little to improve the safety or reliability of the‬
‭system. For-profit companies have a fiduciary duty to maximize profits for‬
‭their shareholders, and any capital spending will increase the rate base and‬
‭subsequently profits. Therefore, if a utility can get capital spending approved,‬
‭it is financially smart to do so, but that doesn’t mean it will be in the best‬
‭interest of ratepayers. Smart but unwise financial investments lead to unjust‬
‭and unreasonable rates.‬
‭Q. What is the role of a rate case and the Commission in addressing this‬
‭contradiction?‬
‭A.‬‭One of the PSC’s obligations is to use the rate‬‭case to interrogate the‬
‭proposed capital expenditures to ensure that any approved capital‬
‭expenditures are the most affordable way to meet the goals of safety and‬
‭reliability as well as a just transition to renewable energy. Another critical‬

‭SARAHANA SHRESTHA‬
‭VI. Central Hudson prioritizes expanding its rate‬
‭base over following the Spirit of the Climate‬
‭Leadership and Community Protection Act‬
‭(CLCPA)‬
‭Q. What does it mean to follow the spirit of the CLCPA?‬
‭A.‬‭The CLCPA is, by intention and design, not limited‬‭to being purely a‬
‭decarbonization goal. By ensuring that 40% of the law’s benefits are realized‬
‭in New York’s disadvantaged communities, the CLCPA is specifically a‬
‭climate justice goal, of which equity is a central component. Therefore,‬
‭following the spirit of the CLCPA means including steps towards equity—and‬
‭the scope of equity included in the law must be seen as a starting point, not the‬
‭ceiling. Additionally, the CLCPA commits to a timeline that is both necessary‬
‭and urgent. Therefore, following the spirit of the CLCPA means also‬
‭demonstrating urgency.‬
‭Q. How does Central Hudson’s Clean Hydrogen Feasibility Study go‬
‭against the spirit of the CLCPA?‬
‭A.‬ ‭The major decarbonization goals of the CLCPA are‬‭to ensure that New‬
‭York’s electricity sector becomes at least 70% renewable by 2030, that the‬

‭VII. Fortis, Central Hudson’s Parent Company, Can‬

‭Just and Reasonable Rates‬
‭Q. What would be just and reasonable rates for Central Hudson?‬
‭A.‬‭To be just is to be morally right and fair, and‬‭to be reasonable is to show‬
‭sound judgment. At a time of an affordability crisis, volatile supply costs,‬
‭large scale billing errors, the need to transition off fossil fuels, and the absence‬
‭of a prudence preceding in regards to Central Hudson’s large scale billing‬
‭errors, the most just and reasonable resolution to this rate case would be a rate‬
‭decrease. Given that access to energy is a basic need for survival, and that‬
‭energy utility bills, unlike other regular bills, are not consistent, the rates must‬
‭be kept as low as possible while delivering safe and reliable service.‬
‭The PSC should dramatically reduce the Company’s return on equity while‬
‭approving appropriate parts of Central Hudson’s capital plan in order to‬
‭ensure necessary grid improvements and safety measures without additional‬
‭cost to ratepayers. Though this case seeks to address only the new rate‬
‭increase requests and is separate from the investigation on Central Hudson’s‬
‭billing issues, the lack of sound judgment the Company’s management has‬

TRANSPORTATION 
4 
Q.    
What types of projects are funded in the “Transportation” category? 
5 
 
The “Transportation” category includes all vehicles, including light and 
6 
heavy-duty vehicles, trailers, forklifts, track/earthmoving equipment, and 
7 
cranes. 
8 
Q. 
What is the Company’s methodology for replacing vehicles/equipment? 
9 
 
The Company uses the following criteria for determining the replacement 
10 
cycle:  Light weight vehicles are included on the replacement listing when 
11 
they are seven years old or have 120,000 miles; Heavy duty vehicles are 
12 
included on the replacement listing when they are ten years old or have 
13 
10,000 machine hours; and other specialty equipment is specifically 
14 
included within the Five-Year Common Capital Plan based on individual 
15 
assessment. 
16 
Q. 
Is it possible for some vehicles/equipment to be replaced (or included on 
17 
the replacement listing) before or after they have met the criteria noted 
18 
above? 
19 
 
Yes, the Company uses the criteria above as the main quantitative 
20 
guidance, however there are also more subjective qualitative factors that 
21 
could result in vehicle/equipment being included on the replacement listing 
22 
A. 
A. 
A. 
107


--- Page 108 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____ 
 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF THE COMMON CAPITAL AND 
OPERATIONS PANEL 
17 
 
either before or after it meets the replacement criteria.  Qualitative factors 
1 
such as significant mechanical component failure, substantial damage 
2 
from accident, severe structural or body corrosion, or obsolescence could 
3 
shorten the service life of a vehicle/piece of equipment.  Qualitative factors 
4 
such as general high-quality condition, and a history of low cost or minimal 
5 
required repairs over its life along with a favorable-type use cycle of the 
6 
vehicle/equipment (i.e., occasional use vehicle/equipment utilized in a 
7 
non-emergency response manner) could extend the service life of a 
8 
vehicle or piece of equipment.

18 
significantly altered the threat environment facing the power grid and

III. REGULATORY GUIDELINES AND FINANCIAL 
CONSIDERATIONS 
Q. 
Please describe the guiding principles to be used in establishing the cost 
14 
of capital for a regulated utility. 
15 
A. 
The foundations of public utility regulation require that utilities receive a 
16 
fair rate of return sufficient to attract needed capital to maintain service to 
17 
customers at reasonable rates.  The basic tenets of this regulatory doctrine 
18 
originate from two decisions by the United States Supreme Court, notably 
19 
Bluefield Waterworks and Improvement Company v. Public Service 
20 
Commission of West Virginia, 262 U.S. 679 (1923) (Bluefield), and Federal 
21 
Power Commission v. Hope Natural Gas Company, 320 U.S. 591 (1944) 
22 
(Hope).  In Bluefield, the Court stated:   
23 
A public utility is entitled to such rates as will permit it to 
24 
earn a return on the value of the property which it employs 
25 
146


--- Page 147 ---
Testimony of Joshua C. Nowak 
Page 7 of 72 
for the convenience of the public equal to that generally 
1 
being made at the same time and in the same general part of 
2 
the country on investments in other business undertakings 
3 
which 
are 
attended 
by 
corresponding 
risks 
and 
4 
uncertainties… 
5 
The return should be reasonably sufficient to assure investor 
6 
confidence in the financial soundness of the utility and 
7 
should be adequate, under efficient and economical 
8 
management, to maintain and support its credit and enable it 
9 
to raise the money necessary for the proper discharge of its 
10 
public duties. 
11 
Later, in Hope, the Court established a standard for the ROE that remains 
12 
the guiding principle for ratemaking regulatory proceedings to this day: 
13 
[T]he return to the equity owner should be commensurate 
14 
with returns on investments in other enterprises having 
15 
corresponding risks.  That return, moreover, should be 
16 
sufficient to assure confidence in the financial integrity of 
17 
the enterprise, so as to maintain its credit and to attract 
18 
capital. 
19 
Q. 
Please explain how these principles apply in the context of the regulated 
20 
rate of return.  
21 
A. 
Regulated utilities rely primarily on common stock and long-term debt to 
22 
finance permanent property, plant, and equipment.  The allowed rate of 
23 
return for a regulated utility is based on its weighted average cost of capital, 
24 
where the costs of the individual sources of capital (i.e., debt and equity) 
25 
are weighted by their respective book values.  The ROE represents the cost 
26 
of raising and retaining equity capital and is estimated with one or more 
27 
analytical techniques that use market data to quantify investor requirements 
28 
for equity returns.  However, the ROE cannot be derived mechanically 
29 
through quantitative metrics and models alone.  To properly estimate the 
30 
147


--- Page 148 ---
Testimony of Joshua C. Nowak 
Page 8 of 72 
ROE, the financial, regulatory, and economic context must also be 
1 
considered. 
2 
Based on the standards established in Hope and Bluefield, the 
3 
authorized ROE in this proceeding should provide the Company with the 
4 
opportunity to earn a fair and reasonable return that is: 
5 
 Adequate to allow the Company to attract the capital that is 
6 
necessary to provide safe and reliable service (the “capital attraction 
7 
standard”); 
8 
 Sufficient to ensure the Company’s ability to maintain its financial 
9 
integrity (the “financial integrity standard”); and 
10 
 At a level that is comparable to returns required on investments of 
11 
similar risk (the “comparability standard”).  
12 
Importantly, a fair return must satisfy all three of these standards.  The 
13 
allowed ROE should enable the Company to finance capital expenditures 
14 
on reasonable terms and provide the Company with the ability to raise 
15 
capital under a full range of capital market circumstances to serve its 
16 
customers.  The DCF and CAPM approaches, while fundamental to the 
17 
ROE determination, are still only models.  The results of these models 
18 
cannot be mechanically applied without also using informed judgment to 
19 
consider economic and capital market conditions and the relative risk of 
20 
Central Hudson as compared to the proxy group companies.  
21 
148


--- Page 149 ---
Testimony of Joshua C. Nowak 
Page 9 of 72 
 
1 
Q. 
Did the Commission conduct a proceeding to review the standard for 
2 
estimating the Cost of Capital for a regulated utility? 
3 
A. 
Yes.  On August 21, 1991, the Commission established the GFP to review 
4 
the Commission’s then-current methodology for estimating the cost of 
5 
equity and to examine various alternatives.1 
6 
 
7 
Q. 
Please provide a brief summary of the purpose of the GFP. 
8 
A. 
The Commission’s goal in opening the GFP was to eliminate controversy 
9 
around ROE calculations and attempt to find common ground on 
10 
contentious issues by developing a consensus approach for setting utility 
11 
equity returns.  Among other things, the Commission questioned whether 
12 
there should be greater consistency in rate of return determinations from 
13 
company to company, such that differences in returns could be directly 
14 
attributed to differences in risk between companies, and whether the 
15 
Commission’s 
historical 
primary 
reliance 
on 
DCF-based 
ROE 
16 
determinations continued to provide fair returns.2     
17 
 
18 
Q. 
Please describe the conclusions outlined in the Generic Finance RD. 
19 
A. 
The Generic Finance RD concluded that the Commission should implement

Q. 
Do the principles and intentions of the Generic Finance RD in the GFP 
18 
require adherence to a static formula? 
19 
A. 
No.  The GFP and the Generic Finance RD did not require strict adherence 
20 
to a static formula, rather, they promoted some basic principles and afforded 
21 
parties the flexibility to investigate approaches to address changing 
22 
financial market conditions.  When faced with the task of estimating the 
23 
152


--- Page 153 ---
Testimony of Joshua C. Nowak 
Page 13 of 72 
cost of equity, analysts are inclined to gather and evaluate as much relevant 
1 
data (both quantitative and qualitative) as can be reasonably analyzed.  
2 
Analysts and academics understand that ROE models are tools to be used 
3 
in the ROE estimation process, and that strict adherence to any single 
4 
approach, or the specific results of any single approach, can lead to flawed 
5 
conclusions.  No model can exactly pinpoint the correct return on equity; 
6 
rather, each model brings its own perspective and set of inputs that inform 
7 
the estimate of ROE.  That position is consistent with the Hope finding that 
8 
“[u]nder the statutory standard of ‘just and reasonable,’ it is the result 
9 
reached, not the method employed, which is controlling.”10  
10 
 
11 
Although each model brings a different perspective and adds depth to the 
12 
analysis, each model also has its own set of inherent weaknesses and should 
13 
not be relied upon individually without corroboration from other 
14 
approaches.  Changes to inputs as a result of changes in economic 
15 
conditions could have widely different effects on the results of the various 
16 
analyses.  Regardless of which analyses are performed to estimate the 
17 
investors’ required return on equity, the analyst must apply judgment to 
18 
assess the reasonableness of results and to determine the best weighting to 
19 
apply to results under prevailing capital market conditions.  No one model 
20 
can reliably and consistently estimate the cost of capital that meets the 
21 
fairness standard of Hope and Bluefield in all market conditions.

19

20

21

22

23 
regulatory decisions should enable the utility to attract capital at reasonable

assessments.

V.   CAPITAL MARKET CONDITIONS 
Q. 
Why is it important to analyze capital market conditions? 
17 
A. 
The ROE estimation models rely on market data that are either specific to 
18 
the proxy group, in the case of the DCF model, or to the expectations of 
19 
 
28  Moody’s Investors Service, Credit Opinion, “Rating Action: Moody's downgrades

market risk, in the case of the CAPM.  The results of the ROE estimation 
1 
models can be affected by prevailing market conditions at the time the 
2 
analysis is performed.  While the ROE that is established in a rate 
3 
proceeding is intended to be forward-looking, the analyst uses current and 
4 
projected market data, specifically stock prices, dividends, growth rates and 
5 
interest rates in the ROE estimation models to estimate the required return 
6 
for the subject company.   
7 
 
 
8

9 
commissions have concluded that current market conditions have affected 
10 
the results of the ROE estimation models.  As a result, it is important to 
11 
consider the effect of these conditions on the ROE estimation models when 
12 
determining the appropriate range and recommended ROE for a future 
13 
period.  If investors do not expect historical or current market conditions to 
14 
be sustained in the future, it is possible that the ROE estimation models will 
15 
not provide an accurate estimate of investors’ required return during that 
16 
rate period.  Therefore, it is important to consider projected market data to 
17 
estimate the return for that forward-looking period.

VI.   PROXY GROUP SELECTION 
Q. 
Please explain why you have used a group of proxy companies to 
2

3 
A. 
In these proceedings, we are focused on estimating the cost of equity for the 
4 
Company’s rate-regulated, electric and natural gas distribution utility 
5 
operations in New York.  Because ROE is a market-based concept and the 
6

7 
companies that are both publicly traded and comparable to the Company.  
8 
Even if the Company was publicly traded entities, it is possible that 
9 
transitory events could bias the Company’s market value in one way or 
10 
another in a given period of time.  A significant benefit of using a proxy 
11 
group is the ability to mitigate the effects of short-term events that may be 
12 
associated with any specific company.  The proxy companies used in my 
13 
ROE analyses possess a set of business and operating characteristics similar 
14 
to the Company’s utility operations, and thus provide a reasonable basis for 
15 
estimating the Company’s ROE.

VII. 
COST OF EQUITY ESTIMATION 
Q. 
How is the required ROE determined? 
18 
A. 
While the cost of debt can be directly observed, the cost of equity and the 
19 
required ROE are market-based and, therefore, must be estimated based on 
20 
 
38 See, e.g., Case 13-E-0030, Proceeding on Motion of the Commission as to the Rates, 
Charges, Rules and Regulations of Consolidated Edison Company of New York, Inc. 
for Electric Service, Testimony of Craig E. Henry, at 14-16. 
179


--- Page 180 ---
Testimony of Joshua C. Nowak 
Page 40 of 72 
observable market information.  The required ROE is determined by using 
1 
one or more analytical techniques that rely on market data to quantify 
2 
investor expectations regarding the range of required equity returns.  
3 
Informed judgment is applied, based on the results of those analyses, to 
4 
determine where within the range of results the cost of equity for a company 
5 
falls.  As a general proposition, the key consideration in determining the 
6 
cost of equity is to ensure that the methodologies employed reasonably 
7 
reflect investors’ views of the financial markets, the proxy group 
8 
companies, and the subject company’s risk profile. 
9 
 
10 
Q. 
What methods did you use to determine the Company’s cost of equity?  
11 
A. 
Consistent with Commission precedent, I used the DCF model and CAPM 
12 
as the primary approaches.  In establishing my recommended ROE, I relied 
13 
on a multi-stage form of the DCF model, and, consistent with the 
14 
Commission’s stated preference, I used both the traditional form of the 
15 
CAPM as well as the Zero-Beta form of that model.  In both forms of the 
16 
CAPM, I incorporated a forward-looking measure of the Market Risk 
17 
Premium.  
18 
 
19 
Q. 
Why do you believe it is important to use more than one analytical 
20 
approach? 
21 
A. 
Because the cost of equity is not directly observable, it must be estimated 
22 
based on both quantitative and qualitative information.  When faced with 
23 
180


--- Page 181 ---
Testimony of Joshua C. Nowak 
Page 41 of 72 
the task of estimating the cost of equity, analysts and investors are inclined 
1 
to gather and evaluate as much relevant data as reasonably can be 
2 
analyzed.  As a result, a number of models have been developed to estimate 
3 
the cost of equity.  For that reason, I use multiple approaches to estimate the 
4 
cost of equity.  However, all of the models available for estimating the cost 
5 
of equity are subject to limiting assumptions or other methodological 
6 
constraints.   
7 
 
8 
Q. 
How are current market conditions affecting the results of the DCF and 
9 
CAPM models?  
10 
A. 
As discussed in Section V, current capital market conditions are heavily 
11 
influenced by monetary policy aimed at mitigating inflationary pressures.  
12 
While long-term interest rates have increased substantially since the 
13 
historical lows of 2020, near-term conditions may not reflect investors long-
14 
term expectations.  Importantly, the risk-free rate in the CAPM analysis 
15 
should also consider projected yields on Treasury bonds, and the market 
16 
risk premium should be based on a forward-looking computation of the 
17 
expected return on the total market less the risk-free rate.  Market risk 
18 
premiums based on long-term historical averages are unresponsive to 
19 
movements in interest rates and would likely understate the market risk 
20 
premium and, accordingly, the cost of equity. 
21 
 
22 
Fluctuations in utility valuations impact the results of the DCF model.  The 
23 
dividend yield is calculated using historical average stock prices, which 
24 
181


--- Page 182 ---
Testimony of Joshua C. Nowak 
Page 42 of 72 
may not fully reflect forward market expectations, especially as utility 
1 
valuations may not reflect the effect of recent increases in interest rates. 
2 
Long-term interest rates have increased substantially since the historical 
3 
lows of 2020 as the Federal Reserve continues to mitigate strong 
4 
inflationary pressures.  Importantly, the CAPM directly accounts for 
5 
changes in interest rates.   These circumstances collectively reinforce the 
6 
importance of using multiple models, as I have with the DCF and CAPM 
7 
approaches.  
8 
       
9 
A. DISCOUNTED CASH FLOW MODEL 
10 
 Q. 
Please describe the DCF approach. 
11 
A. 
The DCF approach is based on the theory that a stock’s current market price 
12 
represents the present value of all expected future cash flows.  In its most 
13 
general form, the DCF model is expressed as follows: 
14 
𝑃଴ൌ
஽భ
ሺଵା௥ሻభ൅
஽మ
ሺଵା௥ሻమ൅⋯൅
஽೙
ሺଵା௥ሻ೙ 
[1] 
15 
Where P0 represents the current market stock price, D1, D2, … Dn are all 
16 
expected future dividends, and r is the discount rate, or required ROE.  As 
17 
discussed below, I have not included the constant growth form of the DCF 
18 
model, but instead have focused on a multi-stage form of the DCF model.   
19 
 
20 
Q. 
Please generally describe the DCF model you relied on.  
21 
A. 
The multi-stage DCF model is an extension of the constant growth form that 
22 
enables the analyst to specify growth rates over multiple stages.  As with 
23 
182


--- Page 183 ---
Testimony of Joshua C. Nowak 
Page 43 of 72 
the constant growth form of the DCF model, the multi-stage form defines 
1 
the cost of equity as the discount rate that sets the current price equal to the 
2 
discounted value of future cash flows.  A multi-stage DCF model addresses 
3 
the possibility that mean five-year growth rates may not be reasonable in 
4 
perpetuity and that payout ratios could vary over time. 
5 
 
6 
Q. 
Please describe the structure of the multi-stage DCF model.  
7 
A. 
The multi-stage DCF model that I have used sets the proxy company’s 
8 
current stock price equal to the present value of future cash flows received 
9 
over three time periods.  In all three periods, cash flows are equal to the 
10 
annual dividend payments that stockholders receive.  The first period is a 
11 
short-term growth period that consists of the first five years; the second 
12 
period is a transition period from the short-term growth rate to the long-term 
13 
growth rate that occurs over five years (i.e., years 6 through 10); and the 
14 
third period is a long-term growth period that begins in year 11 and 
15 
continues in perpetuity.  The ROE is then calculated as the rate of return 
16 
that results from the initial stock investment and the dividend payments over 
17 
the analytical period. 
18 
183

3

4

5

6

12

14 
growth rate will be constant in perpetuity. The multi-stage forms of the DCF 
15 
model, including both the two-stage model that the Commission has relied

17 
recognize short and long-term growth prospects.

Q. 
Does the multi-stage form of the DCF model offer improvements over 
1 
the two-stage model traditionally relied upon by the Commission? 
2 
A. 
Yes.  The general form of the two-stage model relied upon by the 
3 
Commission involves a near-term growth stage based on projected 
4 
dividends and a long-term growth stage employing an estimated long-term 
5 
growth rate in dividends.40  The Commission’s application of a two-stage 
6 
DCF assumes that a company’s growth abruptly shifts to a long-run growth 
7 
state after the initial five-year period.  In contrast, the multi-stage model 
8 
relies on growth rates over three periods, as described above.  The multi-
9 
stage form of the DCF model provides for a gradual transition to a 
10 
company’s expected long-term growth, whereas the two-stage DCF model 
11 
assumes the transition from short to long-term growth occurs in one year.

2 
A. 
As shown in Exhibit __ (JCN-1), I began with the current annualized 
3 
dividend as of May 31, 2023 for each proxy group company.  In the first 
4

5

6

7

8

9

10 
 
11 
Q. 
Why do you believe that earnings growth rates are the appropriate 
12 
growth rates in the DCF model? 
13 
A. 
Earnings are the fundamental driver of a company’s ability to pay 
14 
dividends; therefore, earnings growth is the appropriate measure of a 
15 
company’s long-term growth. In contrast, changes in a company’s dividend 
16 
payments are based on management decisions related to cash management 
17 
and other factors.  For example, a company may decide to retain certain 
18 
earnings rather than include those earnings in a dividend issuance.  
19 
Therefore, dividend growth rates are less likely than earnings growth rates 
20 
to reflect investor perceptions of a company’s growth prospects.   
21

Q.

1

2

3

4

5

6

11

viewpoint of a single analyst.  Therefore, the Commission’s models, which 
13 
have historically relied only on projected dividend per share growth rates 
14 
from Value Line, reflect the growth expectations of a single analyst in the 
15 
first stage of the model.  In contrast, there are several consensus estimates 
16 
of projected earnings per share growth rates that are publicly available and 
17 
widely used by investors, including Zacks Investment Research and First 
18 
Call.  Each of these consensus forecasts considers the growth expectations 
19 
for each company based on the expectations of multiple analysts.  It is not 
20 
reasonable to exclude these timely and widely available sources of

Q. 
Why is the long-term GDP growth rate a reasonable estimate of long-
1 
term growth in the multi-stage DCF model? 
2 
A. 
Long-term estimates of GDP growth are commonly used in regulatory 
3 
proceedings as a proxy for the long-term growth rate in the multi-stage DCF 
4 
analysis.  That application is based on the common theoretical assumption 
5 
that, over the long-run, all companies in the economy will tend to grow at 
6 
the same constant rate.  That assumption is designed to address the 
7 
uncertainty associated with estimating individual company growth rates 
8 
over very long-time horizons and is not meant to suggest that company 
9 
growth rates in the economy will indeed converge in practice over any given 
10 
period.   
11 
 
12 
Q. 
Is your calculation of GDP growth consistent with the way in which 
13 
other analysts’ compute estimates of long-term GDP growth? 
14 
A. 
Yes.  Investors understand that the U.S. economy goes through cycles of 
15 
growth and contraction.  Therefore, it is appropriate to consider the longest 
16 
period possible to measure historical real growth in GDP.  This view is 
17 
consistent with Morningstar’s explanation about measuring GDP growth: 
18 
Growth in real GDP (with only a few exceptions) has 
19 
been reasonably stable over time; therefore, its 
20 
historical performance is a good estimate of expected 
21 
long-term future performance.  By combining the 
22 
inflation estimate with the real growth rate estimate, a 
23 
long-term estimate of nominal growth is formed.56 
24

2

3 
A.

4

5

6

7

11

13

14

15

16 
investors establish long-term growth expectations based entirely on short-
17 
term, company-specific projections.  It is unreasonable to conclude that 
18 
investors would ignore the expectations of long-term macroeconomic 
19 
growth in establishing the long-term growth estimates for an electric or 
20 
natural gas distribution utility or any other company.

B. CAPITAL ASSET PRICING MODEL  
14 
Q. 
Please briefly describe the Capital Asset Pricing Model. 
15 
A. 
The CAPM is a risk premium approach that estimates the cost of equity for 
16 
a given security as a function of a risk-free return plus a risk premium (to 
17 
compensate investors for the non-diversifiable or “systematic” risk of that 
18 
security).60  As shown in Equation [3], the CAPM is defined by four 
19 
components, each of which must theoretically be a forward-looking 
20 
estimate: 
21 
 
60  Systematic risks are fundamental market risks that reflect aggregate economic 
measures and therefore cannot be mitigated through diversification.  Unsystematic 
risks reflect company-specific risks that can be mitigated and ultimately eliminated 
through investments in a portfolio of companies and/or market sectors.

Q. 
What risk-free rate did you use in your CAPM model? 
1 
A. 
I used three estimates of the yield on Treasury bonds: (1) the current three-
2 
month average yield on 30-year Treasury bonds (3.77 percent);61 (2) the 
3 
projected 30-year Treasury yield for 2023-2024 (3.78 percent);62 and (3) the 
4 
projected 30-year Treasury yield for the period 2025-2029 (3.80 percent).63  
5 
In determining the security most relevant to the application of the CAPM, 
6 
it is important to select the term (or maturity) that best matches the life of 
7 
the underlying investment.  As noted by Morningstar: 
8 
The traditional thinking regarding the time horizon of 
9 
the chosen Treasury security is that it should match the 
10 
time horizon of whatever is being valued…  Note that 
11 
the horizon is a function of the investment, not the 
12 
investor.  If an investor plans to hold stock in a company 
13 
for only five years, the yield on a five-year Treasury 
14 
note would not be appropriate since the company will 
15 
continue to exist beyond those five years.64 
16 
Because utility companies represent long-duration investments, it is 
17 
appropriate to use yields on long-term Treasury bonds as the risk-free rate 
18 
component of the CAPM.  In my view, the 30-year Treasury bond is the 
19 
appropriate security for that purpose.  Because the cost of capital is intended 
20 
to be forward-looking, it is appropriate to consider projected measures of 
21 
the market risk premium and interest rates. 
22

Q. 
Please describe your estimate of the market risk premium used in your 
1 
CAPM. 
2 
A. 
The estimated market risk premium is based on the expected return on the 
3 
S&P 500 Index, less the 30-year Treasury bond yield.  The expected return 
4 
on the S&P 500 Index is calculated using a DCF model for all companies 
5 
in the index based on market capitalization-weighted growth rates and 
6 
dividend yields.  The market risk premium implied by each of the three 
7 
Treasury yields discussed above is used in the CAPM analysis. 
8 
 
9 
The Commission previously has relied upon the calculation of a projected 
10 
market risk premium, based on the difference between the estimated 
11 
forward-looking required market return for the S&P 500, as provided by 
12 
BAML, and the risk-free rate.65  As a practical matter, that approach is 
13 
consistent with the Market DCF-derived forward-looking market risk 
14 
premium estimate discussed above (see also Exhibit __ (JCN-5). 
15 
Nonetheless, I have relied on the average of: (1) forward-looking required 
16 
market return for the S&P 500 as calculated using a DCF model for all 
17 
companies in the index; and (2) the estimated forward-looking required 
18 
market return for the S&P 500, as provided by BAML.

Q. 
What Beta coefficient did you use in your CAPM model? 
1 
A. 
I considered the average Beta coefficients for the proxy group companies 
2 
as reported by Bloomberg and Value Line (see Exhibit __ (JCN-4)). The 
3 
Beta coefficients reported by Bloomberg were calculated using ten years of 
4 
weekly returns relative to the S&P 500 Index. Value Line’s calculation is 
5 
based on five years of weekly returns relative to the New York Stock 
6 
Exchange Composite Index. 
7 
 
8 
Q. 
Did you consider another form of the CAPM in your analysis? 
9 
A. 
Yes.  In prior proceedings, the Commission has relied upon the Zero-Beta 
10 
CAPM (the form of which is sometimes referred to as the “Empirical 
11 
CAPM”66) in estimating the cost of equity.  The Zero-Beta CAPM 
12 
calculates the product of the adjusted Beta coefficient and the market risk 
13 
premium and applies a weight of 75.00 percent to that result.  The model 
14 
then applies a 25.00 percent weight to the market risk premium, without any 
15 
effect from the Beta coefficient.  The results of the two calculations are 
16 
summed, along with the risk-free rate, to produce the Zero-Beta CAPM 
17 
result, as noted in Equation [4] below:   
18 
 
ke = rf + 0.75β(rm – rf) + 0.25(rm – rf)  
[4] 
19 
where: 
20 
 
ke = the required market ROE 
21 
 
β = Adjusted Beta coefficient of an individual security 
22 
 
66 See e.g., Roger A. Morin, New Regulatory Finance, Public Utilities Reports, Inc., 
2006, at 189.   
201


--- Page 202 ---
Testimony of Joshua C. Nowak 
Page 62 of 72 
 
rf = the risk-free rate of return 
1 
 
rm = the required return on the market as a whole 
2 
 
3 
In essence, the Zero-Beta form of the CAPM addresses the tendency of the 
4 
“traditional” CAPM to underestimate the cost of equity for companies with 
5 
low Beta coefficients such as regulated utilities.  In that regard, the Zero-
6 
Beta CAPM is not redundant to the use of adjusted Betas; rather, it 
7 
recognizes the results of academic research indicating that the risk-return 
8 
relationship is different (in essence, flatter) than estimated by the CAPM, 
9 
and that the CAPM underestimates the “alpha,” or the constant return 
10 
term.67   
11 
 
12 
As with the CAPM, my application of the Zero-Beta CAPM uses the 
13 
forward-looking market risk premium estimates, the three yields on 30-year 
14 
Treasury securities noted earlier as the risk-free rate, and the Bloomberg 
15 
and Value Line Beta coefficients.  Exhibit __ (JCN-4) show the results of 
16 
the CAPM models.  The traditional CAPM model results range from 10.80 
17 
percent to 10.81 percent.  The Zero-Beta CAPM model results range from 
18 
11.13 percent to 11.14 percent.  The range established by the traditional 
19 
CAPM model and the Zero-Beta CAPM model results is 10.80 percent to 
20 
11.14 percent with a mean of 10.97 percent.

16

17

18

19 
appears that, for whatever the reason, investors during 
20 
this period have seen greater value in utility stocks than 
21 
the DCF methodology would predict.  This suggests that 
22 
the ROE estimated by that methodology may be 
23

Q. 
Are the assumptions used in the CAPM less reliable than the 
4 
assumptions used in the DCF model? 
5 
A. 
No.  As discussed previously, the CAPM relies on a risk-free rate, Beta and 
6 
the MRP.  The risk-free rate is readily observable and can be projected for 
7 
the forward-looking period.  Beta is estimated using the historical 
8 
relationship between the risk of the stock and the overall market.  Finally, 
9 
the market risk premium, while not observable, can be estimated for the 
10 
forward-looking period. My testimony discusses how the current economic 
11 
environment is directly affected by Federal Reserve policy and may not be 
12 
representative of forward-looking market conditions.  Therefore, while the 
13 
CAPM is sometimes criticized as relying on unobservable assumptions, the 
14 
ability to rely on forward-looking assumptions allows for a prospective 
15 
analysis of investors’ long-term expectations.

Q. 
What are the relevant risk factors to equity investors inherent in a 
2 
multi-year stay-out?  
3 
A. 
As described in Section V, inflation and elevated interest rates are the 
4 
predominant factors in the current economic environment.  As such, the 
5 
Company, is exposed to changes in underlying costs that deviate from 
6 
expected levels of inflation.  However, the stay-out premium associated 
7 
with a multi-year rate plan should not only compensate investors for 
8 
changes in the level of interest rates or inflation, but also for the potential 
9 
risk of under-earning that is introduced by “staying out.”  By staying out of 
10 
rate cases, the utility may not fully recover material amounts of capital 
11 
expenditures and may be required to absorb losses due to differences 
12 
between the cost of service established in the rate plan and actual levels of 
13 
revenue and expense.  The premium should compensate the utility and its 
14 
investors for these additional risks over and above interest rate risk.

21 
stay-out premium.  Consistent with prior cases in which a stay-out premium 
22

6

7

8 
a 3.20 percent increase over the prior year.13

13

14 
weaker consumer demand in the face of persistent inflation and higher 
15

16

17

Q. 
Why is net operating income, rather than revenue, the appropriate 
6 
screening criterion to utilize for selecting a proxy group for the 
7

8 
A. 
Net operating income better reflects the contribution of each business 
9

10

11

commodity costs, more closely represents the effect of each business 
17

Q. 
Why is it that current capital market conditions support 
1 
reconsideration of the respective weights placed on the DCF and 
2 
CAPM approaches? 
3 
A. 
There has been an increasing level of complexity and sophistication in 
4 
investors’ analytical approaches over time.  Regulators have recognized 
5 
such complexities and how they may be impacting DCF model results.  
6 
Specifically, regulators have recognized the need to consider multiple 
7 
analytical approaches to develop a reasonable cost of equity. Recognizing 
8 
the important role that dividend yields play in the DCF model, the Federal 
9 
Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) determined that capital market 
10 
conditions have caused the DCF model to understate equity costs for 
11 
regulated utilities.  In Opinion No. 531, the FERC noted: 
12 
There is ‘model risk’ associated with the excessive 
13 
reliance or mechanical application of a model when the 
14 
surrounding conditions are outside of the normal range.  
15 
‘Model risk’ is the risk that a theoretical model that is 
16 
used to value real world transactions fails to predict or 
17 
represent the real phenomenon that is being modeled.23  
18 
 
19 
Given the role that the Federal Reserve has in influencing capital market 
20 
conditions, and its effect on interest rates, it is reasonable to place more 
21 
weight on models that directly account for such inputs.  As discussed in 
22 
Section III, inflation and elevated interest rates are the predominant factors 
23 
in the current economic environment and interest rates are a direct input to 
24 
the CAPM.  As such, the model is more adaptable than the DCF in

Q. 
What are the ratemaking implications of Mr. Yates’s proposal to 
4 
include an ROE update process for each year of the proposed rate 
5 
plan? 
6 
A. 
Mr. Yates is suggesting a solution to a problem that does not exist.  His 
7 
proposal would undermine the potential for settlement agreements and 
8 
multi-year rate plans that are a key feature of the New York regulatory 
9 
environment and introduce both single-issue and retroactive ratemaking.  
10 
Further, Mr. Yates’s proposal would create incremental burdens and costs 
11 
on stakeholders by introducing an additional administrative process. 
12 
 
13 
Q. 
Please elaborate on how Mr. Yates’s proposal would undermine the 
14 
potential for settlement agreements for multi-year rate plans. 
15 
A. 
Settlement agreements represent comprehensive rate plans and include 
16 
agreement on many issues, not just the cost of capital, and represent the 
17 
inevitable give-and-take required to reach a compromise acceptable to all 
18 
parties involved.  One important “give” of a settlement agreement involves 
19 
the Company foregoing the option to file a new rate case in exchange for a 
20 
reasonable assurance of rate certainty.  In doing so, however, a company is 
21 
exposed to changes in the underlying costs that may deviate from expected 
22 
levels of inflation, national and international events, and other unanticipated 
23 
269


--- Page 270 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of Joshua C. Nowak 
Page 56 of 63 
changes such as pandemics.  That is, by staying out of rate cases, the utility 
1 
may not fully recover material amounts of capital expenditures and may be 
2 
required to absorb losses due to differences between the cost of service 
3 
established in the rate plan and actual levels of revenue and expense.  As 
4 
such, the option of seeking rate relief has value.  By foregoing this option, 
5 
equity investors must be compensated for the incremental risk they bear as 
6 
with regard to uncertainty around cost recovery.  Simply put, by requiring 
7 
updates to the cost of equity each year, the Company has less certainty 
8 
associated with its revenues, and therefore has less incentive to enter into a 
9 
settlement agreement. 
10 
 
11 
Q. 
Please describe how Mr. Yates’s proposal constitutes single-issue 
12 
ratemaking. 
13 
A. 
Mr. Yates has focused on a single element of the Company’s total cost of 
14 
service in his proposal to update the cost of equity on an annual basis.  As 
15 
described in my Direct Testimony, the Company’s most recent rate plan 
16 
included a period of historically high inflation, reaching 9.10 percent in June 
17 
of 2022.  The Company had limited protections for cost recovery associated 
18 
with inflation during this period due to the constraints of the rate plan.  Mr. 
19 
Yates’s proposal to expose the Company to changes in the cost of equity 
20 
during the rate plan, but without protections for other macroeconomic 
21 
drivers, such as inflation, introduces single-issue ratemaking that would 
22 
introduce greater risk to shareholders requiring higher returns.  In addition 
23 
270

to adjusting for a single issue, there is an element of retroactivity to his 
1 
proposal.  While resetting the ROE prospectively on an annual basis may 
2 
escape the onus of being classical “retroactive ratemaking” it, nevertheless, 
3 
is still rooted in redress of earnings of the past and abnegation of earnings 
4 
allowances of the past and prior settlement agreements.

statistical analysis used for the study is the retirement rate method,1 which is the 
1 
most commonly used and widely accepted statistical analysis of aged retirements.   
2 
Q. 
Is the statistical analysis the only basis for the service life estimates in the 
3 
depreciation study? 
4 
A. 
No.  While the statistical analysis is an important component of the “life analysis” 
5 
process of depreciation studies, it is only a tool in determining the life 
6 
characteristics that a utility’s assets have experienced historically.  The goal of the 
7 
depreciation study is to estimate the service lives of the assets that are currently in 
8 
service, not those that were retired in the past.  Thus, the process is to develop 
9 
informed estimates of what will occur in the future, not simply to determine what 
10 
has occurred in the past and assume it will recur.   
11 
Q. 
Please continue. 
12 
A. 
The full process of determining the service life estimates is referred to as “life 
13 
estimation.”  Factors other than the statistical analysis should be considered, both 
14 
because the historical statistical data are not always definitive (i.e., often more than 
15 
one survivor curve will represent a similar fit to an original life table, as usually 
16 
only a “stub curve”2 is available for the analysis) and because the historical data 
17 
 
1 The retirement rate method is described in more detail in the Company Depreciation Study filed on 
August 1, 2023 as part of the Company’s electric and gas rate case filings.  
2  A “stub curve” means that the original life table developed from the historical data is not a complete curve, 
i.e. it does not reach 0% surviving.  Because the retirement rate method generally will only produce stub 
curves for many accounts, there is typically an aspect of forecasting or projecting future experience in the 
statistical analysis (even if no other factors are considered).

VI. 
COMPENSATION 
7 
Q.    
Please describe Central Hudson’s overall compensation strategy and 
8 
philosophy. 
9 
A. 
There are several components to Central Hudson’s compensation 
10 
strategy, with each component contributing to the total compensation 
11 
package.  It is this total compensation package (not its individual 
12 
components in isolation) that is evaluated in the employment market.  
13 
Therefore, the Commission should evaluate the Company’s total 
14 
compensation package as a whole rather than consider its component 
15 
parts individually. 
16 
Q.    
Why is it important for Central Hudson to maintain a total compensation 
17 
program that is competitive in the employment market?  
18 
A. 
Maintaining a total compensation program that is competitive in the 
19 
employment market is crucial to Central Hudson’s ability to retain the high-
20 
quality employees it currently employs and to attract high-quality 
21 
candidates for existing or new roles.  The Company’s ability to attract 
22 
342


--- Page 343 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____ 
 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF THE WORKFORCE, COMPENSATION 
AND BENEFITS PANEL 
30 
 
high-quality candidates is imperative not only to meet the incremental 
1 
staffing needs as described in the Panels’ testimony, but also to fill 
2 
vacancies.  Maintaining the competitiveness of Central Hudson’s total 
3 
compensation program has become even more important as the portion of 
4 
the workforce without a defined benefit pension and other post-
5 
employment benefits continues to grow.  Without a market competitive 
6 
compensation and benefits package, these employees are more mobile 
7 
and more likely to consider leaving the Company.  Remaining market 
8 
competitive is crucial to maintaining employee retention and addressing 
9 
the unprecedented rates of attrition that we have recently experienced and 
10 
previously discussed in this testimony.  If Central Hudson is unable to 
11 
maintain a competitive total compensation program, it may put the 
12 
Company’s ability to perform its core functions at needless risk of 
13 
deterioration. 
14 
Q.    
Please describe Central Hudson’s cash compensation program for non-
15 
executive, non-union employees and how Central Hudson manages the 
16 
costs of the program. 
17 
A. 
The Company has adopted a strategy to compensate employees with 
18 
base salaries at the 50th percentile of overall compensation for 
19 
comparable jobs in the Northeast United States.  We employ the services 
20 
of Mercer, a nationally recognized compensation consultant, to establish 
21 
the range of those salaries.  We believe paying at the median level

provides the Company with the ability to attract new qualified employees

2 
median level keeps the Company competitive while also managing 
3 
employee compensation costs in a manner that is reasonable and 
4 
beneficial for customers. 
5 
Q.    
Is the compensation approach applied to Central Hudson’s executives 
6

the median of overall compensation for comparable jobs in similarly sized 
13

Q.    
Has the Commission provided guidelines for recovery of variable 
13

15

17

18

19

20

21 
incentives, is reasonable relative to similarly situated peer companies, or

“The second point we wanted to emphasize is that it is not

SUPPLEMENTAL EXECUTIVE RETIREMENT PLAN 
7 
Q.    
Would you please provide an overview of Central Hudson’s Supplemental 
8 
Executive Retirement Plan (“SERP”)? 
9 
A. 
The SERP is designed to preserve a prior benefit formula for a closed 
10 
group of eligible executives.  The SERP provides the executives who have 
11 
a minimum of 30 years of service at the age of 61 with 57% of their 
12 
pension-eligible earnings (defined as the highest three consecutive 
13 
calendar years during the ten consecutive calendar years immediately 
14 
preceding termination of employment), less the amounts received under 
15 
the Retirement Income Plan and Benefit Restoration Plan.  Individuals 
16 
having less service or retiring prior to age 61 have their benefits reduced 
17 
according to provisions in the SERP. 
18 
Q.    
Are you seeking rate recovery of costs associated with the SERP?  
19 
A. 
Yes.  The Company believes this program is a key component of the 
20 
executive compensation program and delivery rates should be designed to 
21 
allow for recovery of this cost.  Preserving prior benefit formulas for a

VI. 
HEALTH CARE 
9 
Q.    
Does the Company agree with continuation of the use of the gross 
10 
domestic product price index (“GDP-PI”) for health care cost projections 
11 
as part of the general inflation pool items?  
12 
A. 
No.  The Company understands Staff’s long-standing practice is to use the 
13 
GDP-PI, but the policy of doing so was established in 1986 and does not 
14 
adequately consider the trend in increased health care costs that the 
15 
Company continues to experience.  Health care costs are no longer just 
16 
an inflationary item and reflect a key element of expense that continues to 
17 
grow.  As discussed in this Panel’s direct testimony, excluding 2020, the 
18 
three-year average expense growth rate is 12%.  Accordingly, it is likely 
19 
that health care costs will increase at a level that is greater than other 
20 
items in the general inflation pool. 
21 
405


--- Page 406 ---
Case 23-E-0418; Case 23-G-0419 
 
REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF THE WORKFORCE, 
COMPENSATION AND BENEFITS PANEL 
21 
 
Q.    
Is the Mercer study utilized by the Company based on Company-specific 
1 
claims experience?  
2 
A. 
Yes.  While the Company understands Staff’s practice to escalate health 
3 
care costs by the GDP-PI, it is unknown exactly how much of the GDP-PI 
4 
is weighted for health care costs.  What the Company does know is that 
5 
the study conducted by Mercer, as noted in the Panel’s direct testimony, 
6 
shows such costs are projected to exceed GDP-PI.  The GDP-PI is 
7 
determined by a broad measure of inflation while the study was able to 
8 
project costs using the Company’s claims experience and specific trend 
9 
factors.  
10 
Q.    
Does the Company agree that the GDP-PI adequately reflects the 
11 
increase in health care costs? 
12 
A. 
No.  Although health care costs represent a sizable portion of the costs 
13 
included in the GDP-PI, the analysis conducted by our expert consultant 
14 
reflects an increase higher than what the GDP-PI recognized.  
15 
Additionally, GDP-PI includes the costs to produce health care goods and 
16 
services that are broader and differ significantly from the Company’s 
17 
health care costs and include populations covered by government run 
18 
programs such as Medicare and Medicaid. As such, the Company 
19 
maintains that the projection of healthcare costs should be based on the 
20 
Company’s specialized forecast and reliance on the practice of using 
21 
GDP-PI for this expense element should be reconsidered.

5 
 
II. 
CUSTOMER SERVICE PERFORMANCE INDICATORS  
1 
Q. 
What customer service performance indicators are included in the Company’s 
2 
service quality program? 
3 
A.   
Currently, Central Hudson has the following customer service performance 
4 
indicators: (1) PSC Complaint Rate; (2) Residential Customer Satisfaction 
5 
Survey; (3) Percent of Calls Answered by a Representative within 30 seconds; 
6 
and (4) Appointments Kept. (The Customer Experience Panel Direct Testimony, 
7 
at 11-12). In their Rate Plans, the Company is assigned a customer service quality 
8 
performance target for each measure, and if the Company fails to meet the 
9 
performance target(s), then it will incur an NRA. (See Exhibit _ (GCC-2) for a list 
10 
of the Company’s current targets and potential NRAs for each metric.) I further 
11 
note that while the Company’s performance on each metric is measured monthly, 
12 
the target threshold(s) are applied to the average of each Company’s twelve-
13 
monthly scores.   
14 
 
15 
Q. 
Please describe the customer service performance indicators. 
16 
A. 
The PSC Complaint Rate metric measures the number of complaints per 100,000 
17 
customers “charged” to the Company on a monthly basis, but the metric’s target is 
18 
based on the average of twelve-monthly scores. Under the Company’s current rate 
19 
plans, a complaint is considered “charged” when a customer, after first contacting 
20 
the Company to express dissatisfaction with an action, practice, or conduct of the 
21 
490


--- Page 491 ---
 
CASES 23-E-0418 & 23-G-0419 
           
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF 
GREGG C. COLLAR 
6 
 
Company, contacts the Commission to express their dissatisfaction with the 
1 
Company’s resolution of their complaint.  
2 
 
The Residential Customer Satisfaction Survey metric measures the satisfaction 
3 
ratings resulting from a random survey of residential customers who have 
4 
contacted Central Hudson.  
5 
 
The Percent of Calls Answered by a Representative within 30 seconds measures 
6 
the percentage of total calls that are answered within 30 seconds by a Company 
7 
representative.  
8 
 
The Appointments Kept metric is when the Company issues a $20 customer credit 
9 
to a customer when any appointment in which the field employee arrives at the 
10 
appointment outside the scheduled time window.  
11 
 
12 
Q. 
What is the function of customer service performance measures?  
13 
A. 
Customer service performance metrics provide utilities with incentives to provide 
14 
acceptable levels of customer service. Quality service is important to customers 
15 
and serves the public interest. Due to the monopolistic nature of utility service, 
16 
customers cannot select another delivery service provider if they are not satisfied 
17 
with the quality of service they receive from Central Hudson. Meaningful 
18 
measures associated with appropriate financial risk ensure that utility companies 
19 
provide adequate service to their customers. Structured correctly, customer 
20 
491


--- Page 492 ---
 
CASES 23-E-0418 & 23-G-0419 
           
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF 
GREGG C. COLLAR 
7 
 
service performance measures provide utilities with incentives that should result 
1 
in the high level of service to which customers are entitled.  
2

Q. 
Please explain why UIU rejects Central Hudson’s proposals to replace the Central 
4 
Hudson Residential Customer Satisfaction Survey with the statewide customer 
5 
satisfaction survey and to split the Residential Customer Satisfaction Survey into 
6 
two metrics. 
7 
A. 
UIU recommends the Commission reject the Company’s proposal to replace the 
8 
Central Hudson Residential Customer Satisfaction Survey with the statewide 
9 
customer satisfaction survey due to the lack of sufficient historical data, brought 
10 
about by the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic. Central Hudson began 
11 
administering the statewide survey in January 2019 and the ensuing year’s results 
12 
were not only impacted by the pandemic but also by the launch of the Company’s 
13 
SAP-based Customer Information System (CIS). UIU instead proposes the 
14 
Company, Staff, and interested stakeholders convene sometime in Rate Year 1 to 
15 
assess the possibility of replacing the current Residential Customer Satisfaction 
16 
Survey with the statewide customer satisfaction survey and establishing potential 
17 
targets for the new customer service performance measure.  
18 
UIU rejects the Company’s proposal to split the survey into two metrics for a few 
19 
reasons. First, the Company’s proposal would also mean splitting the maximum 
20 
NRAs currently at risk for the Residential Customer Satisfaction Survey. 
21 
495


--- Page 496 ---
 
CASES 23-E-0418 & 23-G-0419

GREGG C. COLLAR 
11 
 
Currently, the maximum amount at risk for the Residential Customer Satisfaction 
1 
Survey is 15 BPs. Whereas if the Company’s proposal were to be adopted, that 15 
2 
BPs would be split evenly between the two new metrics, leaving the Company 
3 
only at risk of 7.5 BPs per survey metric. This is basically shifting some of the 
4 
Company’s NRA exposure due to the splitting of the transaction types, and thus 
5 
reducing the Company’s exposure for each individual transaction type. Second, 
6 
one cannot be assured that the Company’s lack of clarity on whether an equal 
7 
number of transactions would be surveyed between the two categories could lead 
8 
to the Company gaming or manipulating the results as they pertain to whether it 
9 
meets the target or not. For example, one cannot be assured that the Company 
10 
may have surveyed a lesser number of transactions from the General Accounts 
11 
and Billing interactions category than the High Priority interactions category 
12 
during the launch of its SAP CIS. Furthermore, in the Company’s response to 
13 
UIU IR No. 22, the Company confirms that its proposed targets in 
14 
Exhibit__(CEP-3) did not have a breakdown of the performance separately for the 
15 
proposed High Priority interactions and the General Account & Billing

interactions.

Q. 
How do you typically arrive at your proposed service target levels for a 
13 
company’s customer service performance measures? 
14 
A. 
I review a company’s annual service quality performance data for the last five 
15 
calendar years. In this case, I again referenced data that was provided by the 
16 
Company in response to Staff IR No. 356. I calculate the five-year average and 
17 
then apply two standard deviations. I choose two standard deviations because the 
18 
result is a more reliably accurate reflection of the average. Application of two 
19 
standard deviations in this context is a well-established practice in this industry.

10 
 Q. 
Please explain how EAMs are generally structured?  
11 
A.  
Currently in New York, EAMs are a performance-based ratemaking mechanism 
12 
that provides utilities with a financial incentive if they achieve certain goals. 
13 
EAMs typically have targets for achievement at a minimum, midpoint, and 
14 
maximum level for each calendar or rate year. EAMs were introduced by 
15 
Commission order in 2016; that order appeared to be focused on electric utilities 
16 
but did mention the possibility of exploring EAMs for gas efficiency programs.2 
17 
In 2018, the Commission provided further discussion regarding the EAM 
18 
regulatory construct, stating that: 
19 
 
2 Case 14-M-0101, Proceeding on Motion of the Commission in Regard to Reforming the Energy 
Vision, Order Adopting a Ratemaking and Utility Revenue Model Policy Framework, at 82, fn 95 
(issued May 19, 2016) (“Track Two Order”). 
503


--- Page 504 ---
 
CASES 23-E-0418 & 23-G-0419 
           
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF 
GREGG C. COLLAR 
19 
 
[I]ncentives will be based on performance that demonstrably saves 
1 
money for ratepayers. EAMs will not be an additional cost . . . 
2 
rather, as a rule, they will be used to incentivize cost reductions 
3 
that allow utilities to achieve or surpass their energy savings 
4 
targets with spending below authorize program budgets.3  
5 
 
6 
When structuring an EAM, there are many factors that may impact the ability to 
7 
incent a utility to meet the desired goal and provide net benefits to consumers. 
8 
These factors include but are not limited to: (1) the process used to set the 
9 
baseline and forecasts; (2) the process used to set the targets; (3) the basis points 
10 
allocated to the metric; and (4) the evaluation and verification process used to 
11 
assess and report on the Company’s performance.  
12

implementation 
of 
post-2025

[energy

22

V. 
CDG COSTS 
4 
Q. 
What is Community Distributed Generation, or CDG? 
5 
A.  
CDG enables customers for whom rooftop solar was not a viable option to 
6 
directly participate in and enjoy the benefits of renewable energy programs. As 
7 
part of the CDG program, CDG Sponsors can develop an eligible generation 
8 
project—usually a solar photovoltaic (PV) system connected to a utility 
9 
distribution network—and enroll customers served by that utility as members. 
10 
Members then receive credits on their utility bills for the generation the CDG 
11 
project injects into the utility system. In return, members pay the CDG Sponsor a 
12 
monthly subscription fee, which may be fixed or variable, but that is generally 
13 
designed to be some amount less than the value of the credits the customer 
14 
receives.6  
15 
 
16 
Q. 
Describe how the utilities currently bill customers for CDG. 
17 
A. 
On December 12, 2019, the Commission approved a Net-Crediting model for 
18 
consolidated billing for CDG projects. The new model allows for the CDG 
19 
 
6 Case 15-E-0082, Proceeding on Motion of the Commission as to the Policies, Requirements 
and Conditions for Implementing a Community Net Metering Program, Order Establishing 
Process Regarding Community Distributed Generation Billing, at 1 (issued Sept. 15, 2022). 
508


--- Page 509 ---
 
CASES 23-E-0418 & 23-G-0419 
           
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF 
GREGG C. COLLAR 
24 
 
subscription fee to be included on the customer’s utility bill, so that members 
1 
receive one bill instead of two.7 According to the Company’s response to Staff IR 
2 
No. 302, Central Hudson bills approximately 9,500 of their 16,000 CDG 
3 
customers under a fully automated process and the other 6,500 CDG customers 
4 
are billed through a semi-automated process that still requires a manual step in 
5 
order to provide the credit on the bill.

7

8

9

16 
electric industry trends.

4

5 
ROE is a difference in natural gas revenue requirement of approximately $1.3 
6 
million, or roughly 2.9 percent of the Company's proposed revenue deficiency.  
7 
See Exhibit AJK-7. 
8 
Q. 
IS WALMART RECOMMENDING THAT THE COMMISSION BE 
9 
BOUND BY ROEs AUTHORIZED BY OTHER STATE UTILITY 
10 
REGULATORY COMMISSIONS? 
11 
A. 
No.  Decisions of other state utility regulatory commissions are not binding on 
12 
the Commission.  Additionally, each state utility regulatory commission 
13 
considers the specific circumstances in each case in its determination of the 
14 
proper ROE.  Walmart is providing this information to illustrate a national 
15 
customer perspective on industry trends in authorized ROE.

IV. Stay-Out Premium 
12 
Q. 
WHAT IS YOUR UNDERSTANDING OF THE COMPANY'S 
13 
PROPOSED STAY-OUT PREMIUM? 
14 
A. 
The Company proposes that the Commission award a 50 basis point premium 
15 
to the Company's ROE in the event that a multi-year rate plan is reached.  See
16 
Direct Testimony of Joshua C. Nowak, page 70, line 22 to page 71, line 2. 
17 
Q. 
WHY DOES THE COMPANY PROPOSE A STAY-OUT PREMIUM? 
18 
A. 
According to the Company witness Nowak, a stay-out premium is necessary to 
19 
compensate investors for changes in interest rates, inflation, and differences 
20 
553


--- Page 554 ---
Cases 23-E-0418 and 23-G-0419 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF ALEX J. KRONAUER 
23 
between forecasted and actual revenues and expenses.  See id., page 70, lines 4-
1 
15.
2 
Q. 
WHAT JUSTIFICATION DOES THE COMPANY OFFER FOR ITS 
3 
SPECIFIC STAY-OUT PREMIUM OF 50 BASIS POINTS? 
4 
A. 
The Company does not provide justification for its specific 50-basis point stay-
5 
out premium, aside from that is a "…reasonable, albeit conservative, reflection 
6 
of the incremental risk to the Company under a multi-year stay-out provision."  
7 
See id., page 70, line 24 to page 71, line 2. 
8 
Q. 
DOES WALMART HAVE ISSUES WITH THE COMPANY'S 
9 
PROPOSED STAY-OUT PREMIUM? 
10 
A. 
Yes, for two reasons.  First, a multi-year rate plan benefits the Company if 
11 
actual returns on capital are greater than forecasted.  Under the Company's 
12 
proposal, the Company would gain from an additional ROE premium, and also 
13 
potentially from any favorable forecast variances.  There is no need to provide 
14 
the Company with such potentially duplicative relief.  Second, both the 
15 
Company and other New York electric and natural gas utilities have had several 
16 
multi-year rate plans, and their respective authorized ROEs, approved by the 
17 
Commission.  As such, it can be inferred that any ROE premium the 
18 
Commission deems appropriate is already built in to Commission-awarded 
19 
ROEs.

DIRECT TESTIMONY OF LISA V. PERRY 
12 
Q. 
HOW DOES THE COMPANY DETERMINE THE NATURE OF COSTS 
1 
INCURRED BY ITS CUSTOMERS AND HOW THOSE COSTS ARE 
2 
ALLOCATED 
AND 
RECOVERED 
FROM 
THE 
VARIOUS 
3 
CUSTOMER CLASSES? 
4 
As discussed by the Company's Cost of Service Panel, when preparing a COSS, 
5 
the Company first assigns costs to the portion of the Company's system that 
6 
created the relevant cost, which is generally production-related, transmission-
7 
related, or distribution-related.14 This process is call functionalization.15 Within 
8 
each function, the Company then classifies each cost as either demand-related, 
9 
energy-related, or customer-related.16 As explained by the Company, demand-
10 
related costs vary in proportion to the rate and are recovered on a $/kW basis, 
11 
while energy-related costs vary in proportion to the volume of electricity 
12 
delivered, and is expressed as a $/kWh charge.17 Lastly, the Company allocates 
13 
each functionalized and classified cost among the customer classes based on 
14 
either the class's contribution to peak demand ($/kW), contribution to the total 
15 
volume of electricity delivered ($/kWh), or contribution to number of total 
16 
customers. 
17 
14 See COSP Direct, p. 9, line 21 to p. 10, line 9. 
15 See id. 
16 See id. at  11, lines 5-6. 
17 See COSP Direct id. at lines 5-11. 
569


--- Page 570 ---
Cases 23-E-0418 and 23-G-0419 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF LISA V. PERRY 
13 
Q. 
YOU MENTIONED THAT THE SECONDARY DEMAND AND 
1 
PRIMARY DEMAND RATES INCLUDE CUSTOMER, DEMAND, AND 
2 
ENERGY CHARGES. DOES THIS RATE STRUCTURE ALIGN WITH 
3 
HOW THESE COSTS ARE INCURRED? 
4 
A.  
No, they do not. As I briefly mentioned above, certain customers under the 
5 
Secondary Demand and Primary Demand rates, including Walmart, take only 
6 
delivery service from the Company, which are typically classified as demand-
7 
related costs, or costs that do not vary with the amount of electricity provided. 
8 
And, in fact, the Company states that it allocated costs functionalized as "power 
9 
supply transmission" and "distribution-related" using demand allocators that are 
10 
based on each class's contribution to system peaks.18 Because of the fixed nature 
11 
of these costs, in order to align recovery of those costs with how they are 
12 
incurred, delivery service charges should be recovered from customers who 
13 
take service under the Secondary Demand and Primary Demand rates through 
14 
the demand, or $/kW, charge and not through the energy, or $/kWh, charge, as 
15 
proposed by the Company. 
16 
18 See COSP Direct, p. 12, lines 10-15. 
570


--- Page 571 ---
Cases 23-E-0418 and 23-G-0419 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF LISA V. PERRY 
14 
Q. 
DOES THE RECOVERY OF DEMAND-RELATED COSTS THROUGH 
1 
ENERGY CHARGES DISADVANTAGE HIGHER LOAD FACTOR 
2 
CUSTOMERS? 
3 
A. 
Yes. The shift in demand-related costs from per kW demand charges to per kWh 
4 
energy charges results in a shift in demand cost responsibility from lower load 
5 
factor customers to higher load factor customers. This results in a misallocation 
6 
of cost responsibility as higher load factor customers overpay for the demand-
7 
related costs incurred by the company to serve them. In other words, higher load 
8 
factor customers are paying for a portion of the demand-related costs that are 
9 
incurred to serve lower load factor customers simply because of the manner in 
10 
which the Company collects those costs in rates.  
11 
Q. 
WOULD THE PROPER COLLECTION OF DEMAND-RELATED 
12 
COSTS THROUGH A DEMAND CHARGE PROVIDE THE COMPANY 
13 
BENEFITS? 
14 
A. 
Yes. By collecting more demand-related costs through the energy delivery 
15 
charge, the Company could be more susceptible to weather-related and other 
16 
fluctuations in usage than it would be if those costs were recovered through a 
17 
demand charge. A rate design that properly collects fixed costs through a $/kW 
18 
demand charge and energy-related costs through $/kWh variable charges 
19 
should provide greater revenue certainty and more stable utility earnings. 
20 
571


--- Page 572 ---
Cases 23-E-0418 and 23-G-0419

Q. 
WHAT IS YOUR RECOMMENDATION TO THE COMMISSION ON 
1 
THIS ISSUE? 
2 
A. 
For purposes of this case, Walmart proposes that, for a revenue increase to the 
3 
Secondary Demand and Primary Demand schedules, the Commission approve 
4 
the Company's proposed customer charges and assign the remaining increase 
5 
only to the demand charge, such that the delivery energy charges for each 
6 
schedule remain at current levels.  If the Commission were to approve a revenue 
7 
decrease for the schedules, the decrease should be applied only to the delivery 
8 
energy charges for each schedule.

A.

9 
A.

10 
is to promote and defend the legal rights of residential utility consumers by educating the 
11 
public, regulators, and elected officials about the impacts of utility rates, conducting 
12 
research on the rights and energy burden of utility consumers, and through advocacy, 
13 
emphasizing the rights and needs of low-income utility consumers.  I have been employed 
14 
by PULP in various capacities since July of 1990.  I am currently Director of Research for 
15 
PULP.

Overview

Purpose Of Testimony 
2 
Q.  
What is the purpose of your testimony in these proceedings? 
3 
A. 
The purpose of my testimony is as follows: 
4 
1. To address uncertainties about unresolved aspects of the Commission’s ongoing 
5 
investigation into problems involving the September 1, 2021, deployment by 
6 
Central Hudson of its new Customer Information and Billing System (“CIS”) —
7 
uncertainties that make it difficult for me to place reliance on the Company’s filings 
8 
in these proceedings.1,2 Many of the observations, findings, and recommendations 
9 
I make in my testimony must be considered in light of the possibility that a prudence 
10 
review, as strongly urged by PULP3 and the Department of Public Service’s 
11 
(“DPS”) Office of Investigations and Enforcement (“OIE”),4 may be conducted 
12 
subsequent to the date of my testimony, and that the findings of such a review could 
13 
result in the need for updates to Central Hudson’s filings. In my opinion findings 
14 
of this nature would help resolve outstanding issues pertaining to the CIS 
15 
implementation and should therefore be made publicly available before any 
16 
decisions are made involving a multi-year settlement in these proceedings.  
17 
2. To provide evidence demonstrating that the affordability of electric and gas utility 
18 
service rendered by the Company to a potentially large number of low-income

Findings 
13 
Q.  
What are the major findings of your testimony in these proceedings? 
14 
A. 
My testimony examines data reliability issues and affordability and customer service 
15 
matters in several areas including but not limited to evidence that: 
16 
1. Uncertainties arising from unresolved aspects of the Commission’s ongoing 
17 
investigation into problems involving the September 1, 2021, deployment by Central 
18 
Hudson of a new CIS make it difficult to place any reliance on the data included in the 
19 
Company’s filings in these proceedings. Key aspects underlying this uncertainty relate 
20 
to expenses and capital investments that Central Hudson may have incurred, or may 
21 
incur, imprudently in the development of its CIS system, but that may not have been 
22 
sufficiently identified or excluded from consideration in Central Hudson’s proposals. 
23 
It also involves the failure of the Company in its filings to acknowledge that some 
24 
portion of its arrears accumulation after August 2021, may relate to problems with the 
25 
September 1, 2021, CIS launch; and the extent to which these problems may have 
26 
contributed to the Company’s deteriorating credit metrics. 
27 
593


--- Page 594 ---
TESTIMONY OF WILLIAM D. YATES, CPA - CASES 23-E-0418 et al. 
9 
 
2. Under the Company’s one-year proposal, the monthly electric delivery bill increase for 
1 
residential customers would be 31.9%. For residential gas, the increase would be 
2 
29.2%. Gas customers with monthly usage at or above 200 cubic feet (“Ccf”) would 
3 
experience at least a 40% increase in their delivery bills. Central Hudson also proposes 
4 
to raise monthly fixed charges for both electric and gas service.    
5 
3. Gas energy affordability program (“EAP”) participants, especially heating customers, 
6 
would be exposed to detrimental increases in their energy burdens as a result of the 
7 
Company’s requested rate increases. Central Hudson proposes to lower gas bill 
8 
discounts based on its projection that EAP spending would exceed the “2% cap” on 
9 
EAP budgets set by Commission orders in Case 14-M-0565. (Forecasting and Rates 
10 
Panel at 66 – 67) Approximately 4,200 “Tier 3” gas heating participants (80% of total) 
11 
would experience 140% average monthly delivery bill increases under this proposal, 
12 
which would occur against the backdrop of average EAP participant arrears having 
13 
progressed from about $800 prior to the COVID-19 pandemic and $600 in the 
14 
aftermath of Phase 1 arrears relief, to more than $1,100 for the year ended September 
15 
2023. 
16 
4. Despite the Commission’s efforts in 2022 and 2023 to provide extensive arrears relief 
17 
to residential customers impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic, the average number of 
18 
residential customers in arrears who are not EAP participants (“Non-EAP customers”), 
19 
and the amounts they owe, far exceeds June 2022 (“peak pandemic”) levels, even after 
20 
the application Phase 2 arrears relief. During the twelve months ended September 2023, 
21 
an average of almost 55,000 Non-EAP customers had arrears over 60 days old, owing 
22 
an average of about $77 million. These amounts are approximately 222% and 1,442% 
23 
higher than the number of customers in arrears and their amounts owed in the twelve 
24 
months leading up to the Pandemic. 
25 
5. I estimate that the approximately 58,700 low-income households in the Central Hudson 
26 
service area who reported a monthly utility electric or gas bill for in their responses to 
27 
the 2021 American Community Survey incurred a total energy burden — which 
28 
includes electric and gas utility costs, plus the cost of deliverable fuels — averaging 
29 
12% of their incomes, twice the Commission’s maximum 6% of household income 
30 
594

target (hereinafter “six percent of income target” or “6% target”). About 40,800 (70%) 
1 
of these households reported energy burdens greater than the 6% target. I further 
2 
estimate that about 27,900, or 48%, of these households reported total energy burdens 
3 
exceeding ten percent (10%) of their incomes, indicating that they were “severely 
4 
burdened”5 by their energy costs. 
5 
6. It is not clear that the Company has adequately considered Section 7(3) of the CLCPA6 
6 
in developing their proposals in these proceedings by, for example, assessing the 
7 
potentially disproportionate impact that their rate increase requests could have upon the

fifty-three (53) disadvantaged communities (“DACs”) I estimate are included in their

service area. Central Hudson does not maintain data on its service area by census tract,

which is the geographic unit used by the Climate Action Council (“CAC”) in its 2023

12 
communities in New York State.7,8 Many of these communities have elevated DAC-
13 
defined “Energy Poverty / Cost Burden” vulnerabilities that could potentially cause 
14 
them to be disproportionately burdened by the Company’s rate increase requests. 
15

20 
estimate were potentially eligible to participate in Central Hudson’s EAP in 2021 were 
21

8. Central Hudson has the potential ability to develop a highly targeted, community-based

program funded through State budget appropriation that could become effective during
