A. 
I recommend several actions that should be taken to improve utility affordability and 
1 
customer service for many of the Companies’ customers, including but not limited to the 
2 
following: 
3 
1. The findings of a prudence review, as urged by PULP and DPS OIE, involving the 
4 
September 1, 2021, deployment of Central Hudson’s new CIS system, should be 
5 
made publicly available, with such findings being considered before any decisions 
6 
involving a multi-year settlement are made in these proceedings.  
7 
2. In these proceedings, the parties and the Commission should endeavor to limit 
8 
residential bill impacts to the minimum necessary to ensure safe, reliable service at 
9 
just and reasonable rates; and to achieve statewide policy objectives such as low-
10 
income energy affordability and the requirements of the CLCPA. This effort should 
11 
include, but not be limited to: 
12 
 Basing the Company’s authorized ROE upon the Commission’s “Generic 
13 
Financing Methodology”9 in a one-year case. In any multi-year settlement 
14 
resulting from these proceedings, the Company’s ROE for each rate year 
15 
should be set and trued-up based upon, but not exclusively reliant upon, 
16 
updated cost of equity calculations produced by DPS Staff’s GFM. Such a 
17 
framework would include an evidentiary process providing the opportunity 
18 
for all parties to submit interrogatories, file witness testimony and conduct 
19 
cross-examination; and would incorporate separate consideration of all 
20 
factors affecting Central Hudson’s ability to maintain their current credit 
21 
ratings and to raise capital most economically. 
22 
 Exploring alternative rate designs that would, at a minimum, continue the 
23 
freeze on Central Hudson’s monthly fixed charges for electric and gas 
24 
service and, more generally, reward conservation and energy efficiency 
25 
through lower delivery bills; 
26

22

23

25

Low-Income Energy Burdens 
9 
Q. 
Please describe the analysis you undertook of low-income households in the Central 
10

11 
A. 
I analyzed the number of households in the Central Hudson service area who could be 
12 
considered presumptively eligible for non-emergency Home Energy Assistance Program 
13 
(“HEAP”) benefits, by virtue of the income they reported in the U.S. Census Bureau’s 2021 
14

15 
for utility electric or gas service. I estimated that in 2021 (the most current ACS) there were 
16 
approximately 58,700 such households in the Central Hudson service area. (Exhibit 
17 
___(WDY-02) at 2). 
18 
Q. 
What is the American Community Survey ("ACS”)? 
19 
A. 
The ACS is a nationwide, continuous survey designed to provide communities with reliable 
20 
and timely social, economic, housing, and demographic data every year. It is conducted by 
21 
the U.S. Census Bureau throughout the year. ACS questions are designed to provide 
22 
measures of socioeconomic conditions using a weighting method that ensures its estimates 
23 
are consistent with official Census Bureau population estimates by age, sex, race, and 
24 
Hispanic origin, as well as estimates of total housing units. 
25 
The ACS includes questions about the household use and cost of electricity, natural gas 
26 
and deliverable fuels. When combined with household income data, these costs provide 
27 
instructive measures of energy affordability. For example, the federal government uses 
28 
625


--- Page 626 ---
TESTIMONY OF WILLIAM D. YATES, CPA - CASES 23-E-0418 et al. 
41 
 
energy affordability data in the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program 
1 
(“LIHEAP”) to calculate its block grant allocations for each state.38,39 Other federal uses 
2 
include, but are not limited to: 
3 
 The calculation of overall housing cost burdens for purposes of allocating funds for 
4 
the Community Development Block Grants, HOME Investment Partnership 
5 
Program, and Emergency Solutions Grant and Housing Opportunities for Persons 
6 
with AIDS programs; 
7 
 Identification of rental distribution of housing units used to determine Fair Market 
8 
Rents (FMRs); 
9 
 Assessment of poverty, and determination of eligibility for housing assistance 
10 
programs, including the need for housing assistance for low-income, including 
11 
elderly low-income, households; and 
12 
 Estimation of utility costs included in rents for the Consumer Price Index (CPI).

Q. 
Why do you believe that continuing the practice of establishing a fixed ROE including 
1 
an ESM in any multi-year rate plan that may result from these proceedings is not 
2 
likely to be in the public interest? 
3 
A. 
I consider the primary flaw of this framework to be that it establishes fixed ROEs for entire 
4 
rate terms without incorporating any update mechanism to account for changes in 
5 
macroeconomic and investment expectations that impact the Company’s cost of equity as 
6 
realized during the rate plan. For Central Hudson, rate plans have tended to be three years 
7 
in length. In each of the Central Hudson cases I analyzed, for example, a fixed, three-year  
8 
ROE of 9.0% was authorized in Cases 14-E-0318 et al. and 17-E-0469 et al.; and a fixed, 
9 
three-year  ROE of 8.8% was authorized in Cases 14-E-0318 et al.   
10 
Q. 
Why is this a problem? 
11 
A. 
Macroeconomic and utility sector investment considerations, as measured by expectations 
12 
for gross domestic product, inflation, stock prices, dividends, interest rates, the possibility 
13 
of recession, and other factors, changed significantly during the years encompassed by each 
14 
of these rate plans. Reflecting these changes, DPS Staff’s “Generic Finance Model” 
15 
(“GFM”) in rate cases from 2015 through 2023 produced average costs of equity (“GFM 
16 
ROE”) that were lower than authorized Central Hudson ROEs in eight out of eight years. 
17 
In three of these years, authorized ROEs were more than one-half of one percent (50 “basis 
18 
points” or “bps”) higher than the average GFM ROE output produced in subsequent rate 
19 
cases. (Exhibit ___(WDY-03 at 3 - 9). 
20 
Q. 
Why did you look at the GFM ROE output in subsequent cases in order to arrive at 
21 
your findings? 
22 
A. 
As indicated previously, changes in macroeconomic and investor expectations affecting 
23 
the Company’s cost of capital can be readily discerned utilizing output from DPS Staff’s 
24 
Generic Finance Model. The model DPS uses is based on a recommended decision in Case 
25 
91-M-0509, an approach that still guides Commission policy pertaining to utility cost of 
26 
capital.70 Staff’s consistent application of this methodology, adapted over time, in its direct 
27 
 
70 See, Recommended Decision, 7/18/1994, Case 91-M-0509 (Proceeding on Motion of the Commission to Consider 
Financial Regulatory Policies for New York State Utilities), at 31. 
639

55 
 
testimony in rate cases, provides an opportunity to analyze the implicit assumptions 
1 
underlying the fixed ROEs established in successive Central Hudson rate cases in relation 
2 
to the changing expectations of investors as they actually unfolded during the rate years 
3 
comprising these plans. 
4 
 Q. 
What was your conclusion based upon your back-testing of authorized Central 
5 
Hudson ROEs compared to the GFM ROE produced in direct testimony by Staff in 
6 
subsequent cases? 
7 
A. 
I concluded that, taken as a whole, Central Hudson delivery rates from 2015-2023 were 
8 
derived from authorized ROEs that greatly exceeded the developing expectations for 
9 
macroeconomic and utility sector factors impacting the Company’s cost of equity realized 
10 
during these years. Yet there were no adjustments of authorized ROEs during these rate 
11 
plans. The result was that Central Hudson ratepayers incurred up to $35.3 million more in 
12 
the cost of their electric and gas service than they would have if there had been such 
13 
ratepayer protections in place to account for changes in macroeconomic and investor 
14 
expectations during the rate plan. This poor outcome for customers was experienced in 
15 
Cases 14-E-0318 et al. and 17-E-0459 et al. Only during the unprecedented economic and 
16 
financial market fallout associated with the onset and the aftermath of the COVID-19 
17 
Pandemic did this situation abate substantially, as reflected for Cases 20-E-0428 et al. 
18 
(Chart 9). (Exhibit ___(WDY-03) at 3 – 9). 
19 
Q. 
Why didn’t your analysis account for all of the authorized ROEs resulting from multi-
20 
year agreements that were higher than ROEs initially recommended by Staff? 
21 
A. 
My intent was to compare the Company’s authorized ROEs to the objective results of the 
22 
GFM; it was not to compare them to the authorized ROEs of other settled cases. Indeed, 
23 
my analysis seeks to highlight the problem I find inherent in this setting of fixed authorized 
24 
ROEs in multi-year settlements. Comparing authorized ROEs in multi-year settlements 
25 
with each other would have served no purpose in this regard.    
26

27 
A. 
Yes. I deducted any excess earnings shared with customers in arriving at my conclusions. 
28 
Earnings shared with customers amounted to $1.2 million for the period. (Exhibit

2

4 
A. 
No. The $1.2 million shared with customers represented just 12% of the $10.4 million of 
5

6 
through 2023. I do not consider this to be justification for allowing the Company to have

8 
Q. 
Do you think that an ESM in these proceedings will be an effective mechanism that 
9 
mitigates any impact of earnings in excess of GFM output?  
10 
A. 
No. It is unlikely that any ESM in these proceedings will provide equitable sharing in that 
11 
it will likely continue to set a “dead band” above the authorized ROE before any sharing 
12 
occurs. Since 2014, dead bands have been set at 0.5% (50 bps) above authorized ROE. This 
13 
observation alone is evidence that ESMs do nothing to address the fundamental flaw of 
14 
settled rate plans, which is that authorized ROEs are established that are not subject to 
15 
adjustment to account for changes in macroeconomic and investment expectations 
16 
affecting utility cost of equity during the individual rate years of these plans. 
17 
Q. 
For the period you analyzed, what was the breakdown of sharing between 
18 
shareholders and customers of the earnings derived from actual returns exceeding 
19 
authorized returns?  
20 
A. 
In the four years in which Central Hudson actual earnings exceeding authorized earnings 
21 
from 2015 through 2023, I found that out of a total of $10.4 million of such earnings, $9.2 
22 
million, or 88% were retained by shareholders, while only $1.2 million, or 12% were 
23 
shared with ratepayers. (Exhibit ___(WDY-03) at 3 , 6).

Q. 
Would an annual ROE update process address “regulatory lag”?  
9 
A. 
Yes. It would address “regulatory lag” annually; as opposed to the current framework for 
10

11 
only an inadequate, inequitable ESM as a means of sharing the benefits of realized ROEs 
12

16 
2023. While there was some upward variability in GFM ROE in those years, my analysis 
17 
still shows that in no instance would such increases have been more than offset by the 
18

22

23 
recommended ROEs that depart from results produced solely by the GFM; and/or 
24 
adjustments to recommended equity ratios.

allowances proposed by the Revenue Requirements Panel (about $716,000 for Central 
5 
Hudson) in relation to the potential savings to ratepayers that could be achieved by an 
6 
annual ROE update process from 2015 through 2023 (up to $35.3 million, an annual 
7 
average of up to $4.4 million), I believe that the potential benefits to ratepayers would far 
8 
outweigh the possible cost impacts of more frequent rate cases. (Update Exhibits ___(RRP-
9 
2), Schedule A at 4; ___(RRP-3), Schedule A at 3).

Q. 
How would such an annual ROE updating process address the fact that utilities in 
11 
New York, including Central Hudson, very often don’t even earn their authorized 
12 
ROE, and that updating ROEs could further erode their operating performance?  
13 
A. 
Authorized ROE is only one of the factors contributing to operating performance. In my 
14 
opinion, it should have little to do with the separate rate case process of setting allowances 
15 
for recovery of operating costs. Staff recognized the importance of this separation of 
16 
revenue requirement components in its Finance Panel testimony in the most recent 
17 
NYSEG/RG&E cases: 
18 
In the context of Commission rate proceedings, the revenue requirement is the 
19 
dollar amount required by a company to provide service during a rate year. It is 
20 
the amount that will allow the company to recover all of its reasonably expected 
21 
operating costs, including taxes and depreciation. In addition, the revenue 
22 
requirement includes a fair return that will allow the utility the opportunity to 
23 
recover the cost of funds supplied to it by investors.73 (Emphasis added). 
24 
The Commission also recognized the significance of this separation (in particular noting 
25 
the importance of efficient and economic management the utilities it regulates) in Con

Suspension of Service Terminations During Periods of Extreme Weather

Q.

9 
E-0428 et al.88  
10

11 
Hudson agreed to: 
12 
 Accept all HEAP payments and provide the customer with continued service 
13 
regardless of the amount due and/or the customer’s payment status; 
14

15

toward reinstating that agreement with the difference paid by the customer or 
17 
through Department of Social Services emergency grants;

19 
weather forecast predicts below-freezing (32 degrees) temperatures on any given 
20 
day, or predicts “feels like” temperatures at or below-freezing (32 degrees) for 2 or 
21 
more consecutive days; 
22 
 Refrain from locking customers who are coded as Elderly, Blind or Disabled  
23 
(EBD); and 
24 
 Ensuring the safety of Low-Income and EBD customers by not terminating their 
25 
gas service due to non-payment; or their electric service in situations in which they 
26 
 
88 See, Joint Proposal, Cases 20-E-0428 et al, at 62 - 63.

require electricity to sustain their heating source (except on days in November or 
1 
April during favorable weather conditions). 
2 
Q. 
Do you believe these protections should be continued in the Rate Year in these 
3 
proceedings?  
4 
A. 
Yes. Preventing service terminations during extreme cold is a public health, safety, and 
5

6

7 
the risk of hypothermia during cold weather periods increases, as does the possibility that 
8 
customers who have been disconnected will resort to unsafe alternatives for their lighting 
9 
and heating. I therefore recommend that this provision of the 2020 rate case be continued.

11 
A. 
Central Hudson agreed to suspend electric residential service terminations for non-payment 
12 
of service if the: 
13 
 National Weather Service heat index was forecasted to reach 93 degrees or higher, 
14 
including on the calendar day before, in the Company’s service territory; or 
15 
 Actual heat index reached 93 degrees or higher on any given day. 
16 
Q. 
Do you recommend any modifications to Central Hudson’s policy relating to 
17 
residential service terminations during extreme heat?  
18 
A. 
Yes. Preventing service terminations during extreme heat is also a public health, safety, 
19 
and welfare issue.89 Vulnerable customers must be able to rely upon electricity to operate 
20 
their air conditioning units at home. While the Company’s current policy was a good step 
21 
forward, it should be expanded to include days where the heat index is forecast to hit 90 
22 
degrees (including not terminating one calendar day before and two calendar days after 90-
23 
degree days). Additionally, in communities within the Companies’ service areas impacted 
24 
by “Heat Island” effects, I advocate for lowering the threshold temperature for extreme 
25 
heat protections to 85 degrees.

89 See, e.g., https://www.epa.gov/climate-indicators/heat-related-illnesses.

TESTIMONY OF WILLIAM D. YATES, CPA - CASES 23-E-0418 et al. 
72 
 
Q. 
Why do you argue that the overall extreme heat threshold should be lowered to 90 
1 
degrees?  
2 
A. 
Ninety degrees is the threshold used to identify extreme heat conditions by federal 
3 
government agencies such as the Federal Emergency Management Agency (“FEMA”) and 
4 
the Department of Homeland Security.90 It is also the threshold temperature beyond which 
5 
NOAA’s National Weather Service Heat Index indicates extreme caution should be taken 
6 
to avoid heat disorders due to prolonged exposure or strenuous activity.91  
7 
Q. 
Why do you advocate for lowering the threshold temperature for extreme heat 
8 
protections to 85 degrees within communities impacted by “Heat Island” effects?  
9 
A. 
According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”), heat islands are 
10 
urbanized areas that experience higher temperatures than outlying areas. Structures such as 
11 
buildings, roads, and other infrastructure absorb and re-emit the sun’s heat more than 
12 
natural landscapes such as forests and water bodies. Urban areas, where these structures 
13 
are highly concentrated and greenery is limited, become “islands” of higher temperatures 
14 
relative to outlying areas. Daytime temperatures in urban areas are about 1–7°F higher than 
15 
temperatures in outlying areas and nighttime temperatures are about 2-5°F higher.92 
16 
Cities in the Central Hudson service area such as Kingston and Poughkeepsie have 
17 
recognized the current and future extreme heat risks to their populations.93,94 Both have 
18 
established cooling centers for residents to visit during periods of extreme heat. However, 
19 
vulnerable individuals such as the elderly and disabled, as well as many members of low-
20 
income households, may not be able to access such centers.  These vulnerable populations 
21 
are particularly at risk to the effects of extreme heat. For these reasons, I propose that the 
22

https://www.cdc.gov/climateandhealth/pubs/extreme-heat-guidebook.pdf.

11

13 
$277,500, from the appropriate period in the non-major storm restoration

the historic year and Rate Year projection was found and a tax rate of 8%

Q. 
Please provide an overview of the typical 
5 
management and operations audit process. 
6 
A. 
The Commission first initiates a proceeding that 
7 
provides for the issuance of a Request for 
8 
Proposals, referred to as an RFP.  The RFP 
9 
details the scope of work and expected schedule 
10 
for a particular audit.  The Department reviews 
11 
proposals received from consulting firms.  The 
12 
Commission then selects a consulting firm to 
13 
conduct the audit.  The chosen consulting firm, 
14 
the Department, and the utility or utilities 
15 
subject to the audit then enter into a multi-
16 
party agreement that governs the conduct of the 
17 
audit.  The consulting firm develops a work 
18 
plan, interviews company personnel, performs its 
19 
analysis, and submits an audit report to the 
20 
Department.  The Commission then releases the 
21 
report to the public. 
22 
Q. 
What are a utility’s responsibilities regarding 
23 
the outcome of a management and operations audit 
24 
862


--- Page 863 ---
Cases 23-E-0418 & 23-G-0419 
 Staff Management Audit Panel 
9 
 
report? 
1 
A. 
When the Commission issues a management and 
2 
operations audit report, utilities are required 
3 
by PSL §66(19)(b) to file with the Commission an 
4 
implementation plan for the audit 
5 
recommendations.  The Commission may require the 
6 
utility to modify its implementation plan.  Upon 
7 
the Commission’s approval or approval with 
8 
modification, the implementation plan becomes 
9 
enforceable.  Staff monitors the utility’s 
10 
implementation of the audit recommendations 
11 
pursuant to the Commission-approved 
12 
implementation plan.  Utilities are required to 
13 
submit regular implementation updates to the 
14 
Commission, as well as provide evidence to Staff 
15 
that demonstrates implementation, for Staff 
16 
review and approval.  Accordingly, audit 
17 
recommendations generally fall into one of three 
18 
categories of completion status: In Progress, 
19 
Pending Review (reported as complete by the 
20 
utility but under review by Staff), and 
21 
Completed.  Utilities are required to comply 
22 
with the implementation plan until Staff 
23 
determines that all recommendations have been

10

11 
of electric and gas utilities every five years.  
12 
PSL §66(19) further empowers the Commission to 
13 
initiate focused operations audits of one or 
14 
more electric and gas utilities as needed.  Most 
15 
focused operations audits, such as the Staffing 
16 
Audit, are initiated to identify statewide best 
17 
practices or improvements.  However, the 
18 
Commission can also initiate a focused 
19 
operations audit in response to utility actions 
20 
that are adverse to ratepayer interests.  
21 
Examples of such audits include forensic 
22 
accounting investigations, audits resulting from 
23 
customer complaints, and audits intended to 
24

II. 
PURPOSE OF TESTIMONY 
17 
Q.    
What is the purpose of the Finance Panel’s testimony in these 
18 
proceedings? 
19 
A.

20 
capital structure, the cost of debt, and the cost of equity.  Additionally, the 
21 
Panel addresses the importance of the Company’s ability to maintain 
22 
access to the financial markets at a reasonable cost.  Specifically, the 
23 
928


--- Page 929 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____

Panel will discuss: 1) Central Hudson’s recent credit rating downgrades; 2) 
1 
the necessity to maintain access to capital markets and the value of a 
2 
strong credit rating; 3) the importance of avoiding future credit rating 
3 
downgrades by improving the timeliness of cost recovery and increasing 
4 
the Company’s equity ratio; and 4) the drivers of recent interest rate 
5 
increases and the need for an interest rate deferral in order to protect 
6

7 
this testimony will discuss the cost of equity recommendations developed

Q.    
What are the key findings and recommendations within this testimony?   
12 
A. 
The Panel’s testimony discusses the Company’s concerns about its credit 
13 
quality.  During the past two years, the Company has experienced one-
14 
notch credit rating downgrades by Moody’s Investor’s Service and 
15 
Standard & Poor’s.  Most recently, Fitch Ratings changed its outlook on 
16 
the Company to negative, signaling a potential downgrade with particular 
17 
emphasis on the credit supportiveness of future regulatory proceedings: 
18 
The Negative Rating Outlook reflects Fitch’s concerns that, 
19 
absent a significantly improved outcome in the Company’s 
20 
next rate case, CHG&E’s future credit metrics will no longer 
21 
be consistent with the current rating.1 
22 
 
23 
 
1  
Fitch Ratings, “Fitch Revises the Central Hudson Gas & Electric’s Outlook to Negative; 
Affirms IDR at 'BBB+',” January 20, 2023.  Credit report provided in Confidential Exhibit (FP-
2), Schedule C.  
930


--- Page 931 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____ 
 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF THE FINANCE PANEL 
9 
 
The Company operates in the regulated utility industry which is capital 
1 
intensive in nature with investments in infrastructure and systems financed 
2 
by shareholders and debt initially and then reimbursed by customers over 
3 
time.  Like most of the industry, the Company had been able to maintain 
4 
an “A” rating over time due to strong financial metrics based on supportive 
5 
equity ratios and returns, timely cash recovery of operating costs, and a 
6 
supportive regulatory framework.  However, the Company’s metrics have 
7 
been challenged in recent years by federal tax reform; a growing capital 
8 
program needed to maintain reliability, safety and to support New York 
9 
State’s clean energy goals; and the under-collection of major operating 
10 
expenses such as storm restoration costs, energy efficiency programs, 
11 
and heat pump programs.  These factors in conjunction with growing 
12 
customer arrears and the reduction of the equity ratio from 50% to 48% 
13 
has resulted in weakened cash flow metrics.  To avoid continued 
14 
deterioration, steps need to be taken to address these issues.  If not 
15 
properly remedied, further downgrading of the Company’s ratings will 
16 
result in a higher cost for customers over the long term and could limit the 
17 
Company’s access to reasonably priced capital during market restrictions.  
18 
To maintain a better balance consistent with the Company’s continued 
19 
objective of maintaining an “A” credit rating, as supported in Case 12-M-
20 
0192, the Company proposes returning the allowed equity ratio to 50%, 
21 
setting the allowed return on equity at 9.8%, and significantly improving 
22 
the timeliness of cost recovery for storm restoration, energy efficiency, and 
23 
931


--- Page 932 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____ 
 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF THE FINANCE PANEL 
10 
 
heat pump programs.  Finally, supportive regulatory mechanisms such as 
1 
the Rate Adjustment Mechanism (“RAM”) surcharge, as described in the 
2 
testimony of the Forecasting and Rates Panel, are essential in order to 
3 
provide more timely recoveries of necessary cash outlays.  Timely 
4 
recovery of such expenses and the improvement of Central Hudson’s 
5 
credit metrics is aligned with the long term interests of our customers and 
6 
other stakeholders. 
7 
III. 
FINANCIAL INTEGRITY 
8 
Q.    
What are Central Hudson’s financial integrity objectives? 
9 
A. 
Central Hudson defines financial integrity as maintaining a financial profile 
10 
that supports a strong credit rating in the “A” category, which in turn 
11 
supports adequate access to capital at reasonable prices.  Central 
12 
Hudson has a long-standing objective and commitment to maintaining a 
13 
sound, creditworthy financial structure.  This commitment is not only 
14 
ideological, but also practical as it balances two key responsibilities: the 
15 
obligation to provide safe and reliable service to our customers and to do 
16 
so at a reasonable price. 
17 
Q.    
Is access to sufficient financial resources during varying economic 
18 
climates critical to the Company’s ability to provide service?  
19 
A. 
Yes.  As we noted, the Company has an obligation to provide safe and 
20 
reliable service to our customers.  In order to meet this obligation, the 
21 
Company must have access to sufficient cash and credit at all times 
22 
932


--- Page 933 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____ 
 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF THE FINANCE PANEL 
11 
 
regardless of prevailing economic conditions and in both supportive and 
1 
restrictive market conditions.     
2 
Q.    
Do you have examples demonstrating why access to cash and credit are 
3 
critical for Central Hudson? 
4 
A. 
Yes.  Central Hudson continues to purchase large quantities of electricity 
5 
and natural gas on behalf of its customers who have not elected to receive 
6 
their supply from an energy service company.  The quantities can vary 
7 
based on customer usage and are often driven by weather-related 
8 
(temperature) end-uses like air conditioning and heating.  The price of 
9 
electricity and natural gas can also vary considerably in response to a 
10 
range of factors, including but not limited to market supply and demand 
11 
conditions.  In the past two years, energy prices have increased by 132% 
12 
and based on market forecasts, are expected to remain above historic 
13 
levels for the foreseeable future.  The supply cost increases negatively 
14 
impact cash flows as the Company pays for supply in advance of the 
15 
collection of receipts from its customers.  Therefore, Central Hudson must 
16 
maintain adequate access to cash or credit to meet its unpredictable and 
17 
varying daily supply needs.  The Company must also maintain financial 
18 
flexibility to serve all customers as the utility is the required provider of last 
19 
resort.  Therefore, the Company must have the financial flexibility to serve 
20 
customers who terminate supply from energy service companies or where 
21 
an energy service company fails, resulting in customers defaulting back to 
22 
supply from Central Hudson.  Additionally, the Company must have 
23 
933


--- Page 934 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____ 
 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF THE FINANCE PANEL 
12 
 
sufficient resources to address unexpected events that create financial 
1 
strains, such as spikes in inflation or other economic upheaval, restoration 
2 
activities during and after major storms or serial minor storms and, most 
3 
recently, the lingering impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the 
4 
Company’s operations.   
5 
Q.    
How do storms impact Central Hudson’s financial integrity? 
6 
A. 
When Central Hudson expects to experience a severe storm event that 
7 
causes significant service interruptions, it begins mobilization of mutual 
8 
assistance to restore service to its customers as quickly and safely as 
9 
possible.  It is imperative that the Company has immediate and ready 
10 
access to cash to fund these restoration activities.  Any delay in 
11 
restoration caused by limited or a total lack of access to financial 
12 
resources is an unacceptable situation.  Moreover, the ability to 
13 
temporarily finance such outlays at a reasonable cost is critical since 
14 
recovery is not immediate.  Recovery has historically lagged because 
15 
expenditures have significantly exceeded the rate allowance.  Although 
16 
the RAM as approved in the Order in Cases 17-E-0459 and 17-G-0460 
17 
has provided some near term recovery, more timely recovery of these 
18 
operating costs is needed to support financial integrity and prevent further 
19 
deterioration in the Company’s credit ratings.  
20 
Q.    
How has the COVID-19 pandemic created financial strain, impacting 
21 
Central Hudson’s operations and financial integrity? 
22 
934


--- Page 935 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____ 
 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF THE FINANCE PANEL 
13 
 
A.

18

19

20

21

23

interest on debt and, as a result, the weighted average pre-tax cost of

2 
distress drove the cost of both debt and equity and, consequently, the pre-
3 
tax cost of capital upward rapidly.  Parties in the Generic Finance Case 
4 
concluded that an “A” bond rating was the appropriate target for electric 
5 
and gas utilities and submitted a formal proposal to adopt that target.

Q.    
Please provide an overview of the quantitative analysis performed by the 
7 
credit rating agencies when assessing a utility’s credit quality.  
8 
A. 
Financial ratios are the key determinants used in the quantitative 
9 
assessment by credit ratings agencies.  Moody’s assessment is based on 
10 
four financial ratios comprising 40% of the agency’s rating factors:21  1) 
11 
cash flow interest coverage; 2) cash flow to total debt; 3) financial 
12 
leverage; and 4) balance sheet leverage.  S&P’s rating methodology 
13 
initially gives equal weight to a company’s business risk profile and its 
14 
financial risk profile, before applying potential modifiers.  The financial risk 
15 
profile is measured by two core credit ratios: 1) cash flow to total debt; and 
16 
2) debt to earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization 
17 
(“EBITDA”).  S&P also considers five supplemental ratios (three payback 
18 
ratios and two coverage ratios that consider a utility’s ability to make 
19 
payments of interest and principal on outstanding debt) as part of its 
20 
 
21  The weighting on these four ratios increased from 30% to 40% in Moody’s December 2013 
update to its rating methodology.  Prior to that, a liquidity assessment contributed an 
independent 10% in Moody’s rating methodology.  Liquidity is now included in the qualitative 
considerations in the ratings analysis. 
957


--- Page 958 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____ 
 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF THE FINANCE PANEL 
36 
 
quantitative analysis.  Fitch’s rating methodology includes three debt 
1 
leverage and coverage ratios:  1) debt to EBITDA; 2) debt to funds from 
2 
operations; and 3) funds from operations to interest and fixed charges.  
3 
Published credit rating methodologies for all three of the agencies are 
4 
included in Confidential Exhibit __ (FP-2).  
5 
Q.    
Is there a common theme in the quantitative analyses employed by the 
6 
credit rating agencies when determining bond ratings? 
7 
A. 
Yes, the results obtained from the majority of quantitative measures 
8 
employed to assess credit quality are driven by the level of debt leverage 
9 
at the subject utility and the amount of debt leverage included in the 
10 
ratemaking capital structure.  The corollary to this is that the amount of 
11 
common equity maintained by the subject utility and the amount of 
12 
common equity in the ratemaking capital structure also drive the 
13 
quantitative measures considered by the credit rating agencies.    
14 
Q.    
How does the Company’s equity ratio affect the quantitative assessment 
15 
of the Company’s credit quality? 
16 
A. 
A Company’s equity ratio affects both operating income and debt 
17 
leverage.  Operating income improves due to the application of the ROE 
18 
to the incremental equity and a concomitant reduction in interest expense 
19 
on debt.  In addition, the capitalization has less leverage which is another 
20 
key component in assessing financial risk in credit analysis.  The 
21 
combination of higher operating income and lower levels of debt leads to 
22 
improvement in interest coverage ratios, leverage ratios, and payback 
23

VIII. 
COST OF DEBT 
3 
Q. 
What exhibits have you prepared to further explain the cost of debt 
4 
proposed in this case? 
5 
A. 
Exhibit __ (FP-6) contains two schedules that address the development of 
6 
the cost of debt.  Schedule A shows the Company’s projected average 
7 
long-term debt for the three twelve-month periods ending June 30, 2025, 
8 
June 30, 2026, and June 30, 2027.  Schedule B shows the forecast of 
9 
interest rates for 2023 through 2027 used to calculate interest expense on 
10 
projected debt issuances.   
11 
Q. 
Please discuss Exhibit __ (FP-6) in more detail. 
12 
A 
For each of the twelve-month periods presented in Schedule A, a 
13 
complete portfolio of Central Hudson’s long-term debt is shown.  New 
14 
long-term debt issued in each period matches the financing program 
15 
shown in Exhibit __ (FP-4), Schedule A.  For existing debt, the interest 
16 
rate shown reflects the actual coupons on the debt.  For new issuances, 
17 
the interest rate reflects the projections in Schedule B.  Central Hudson 
18 
also has two series of variable rate debt:  1999 Series B and 2014 Series 
19 
E.  The 2014 Series E matures in March 2024.  The forecasted interest 
20 
rates for the 1999 Series B is reflected in the projections in Schedule B.  In 
21 
practice, Central Hudson issues debt at par without discounts or 
22 
970


--- Page 971 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____ 
 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF THE FINANCE PANEL 
49 
 
premiums.  Therefore, the amortizations shown primarily reflect the 
1 
expenses associated with the issuance of debt and the continued 
2 
amortization of expenses related to retired debt, where applicable, 
3 
resulting in a total average cost of debt of 4.39% in the Rate Year.   
4 
Q. 
What treatment do you recommend to account for variations in interest 
5 
rates from your projections? 
6 
A. 
Central Hudson has had longstanding deferral accounting treatment for 
7 
the interest expense on its variable rate bonds.  This has enabled the 
8 
Company to realize the cost benefits for its customers of short-term 
9 
interest rates with the protection from changes in those rates over time.  
10 
We recommend that the deferral treatment adopted in Cases 20-E-0428 
11 
and 20-G-0429 continue for this debt, including the impact of refinancing 
12 
such debt.  Central Hudson keeps interest rate caps on its variable rate 
13 
bonds, protecting against unexpected increases in rates for periods from 
14 
one to three years.  Additionally, its variable rate bonds are callable for 
15 
optional refinancing should conditions warrant it. 
16 
Q. 
What about the interest rates on newly issued long-term debt? 
17 
A. 
Most of Central Hudson’s long-term debt is comprised of bonds with fixed 
18 
interest rates.  Projected debt costs reflect these rates for all existing debt.  
19 
For projected new issuances of long-term debt, there is a chance that 
20 
actual interest rates will vary from those assumed since future interest 
21 
rates are nearly impossible to predict, particularly in the near term given 
22 
the continued uncertainty in the financial markets and potential actions of 
23 
971


--- Page 972 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____ 
 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF THE FINANCE PANEL 
50 
 
the Federal Reserve to curb inflation.  Because of the relatively small size 
1 
of our debt issuances, Central Hudson is a price-taker as a debt issuer in 
2 
the financial markets.  Our goals are to manage volatility, minimize 
3 
refinancing risk, and achieve a reasonable cost of long-term debt over 
4 
long periods of time.  We do this by issuing mostly fixed rate debt, 
5 
managing our maturity schedule, issuing long-dated maturities when 
6 
market interest rates are low and issuing shorter maturities when market 
7 
interest rates are high.  We can do this most effectively when there is no 
8 
interest expense impact driven by differences in actual interest rates at the 
9 
time of issuance compared to those assumed in delivery rates.  Since we 
10 
have no control over the market and given the recent volatility, an interest 
11 
rate true-up should be adopted for debt issued during the term of the rate 
12 
agreement, using deferral accounting treatment to record the expense 
13 
impact of favorable or unfavorable variations in the weighted average cost 
14 
of the fixed rate debt shown in our exhibits (or the rate ultimately reflected 
15 
in delivery rates as a result of these proceedings).   
16

COST OF COMMON EQUITY 
17 
Q. 
What is the basis for adopting 9.8% as Central Hudson’s cost of equity? 
18 
A. 
Based on the quantitative and qualitative analyses discussed throughout 
19 
Witness Nowak’s Direct Testimony, we conclude that an appropriate and 
20 
conservative ROE is within the range of 9.85% and 10.71%.  However, the 
21 
analytical results yield a significant increase from the 9.0% ROE reflected 
22 
972


--- Page 973 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____

51 
 
in the Company’s current delivery rates and would drive a corresponding 
1 
increase in such rates.  For purposes of mitigating the proposed rate 
2 
increase, the Company is proposing an ROE of 9.8%, which is below the 
3 
entirety of the ranges presented by Mr. Nowak.  This proposed ROE is 
4 
near the lower bound of Mr. Nowak’s recommended range and limits the 
5 
impact on delivery rates in recognition of the lingering economic impacts 
6 
on customers following COVID-19 and current high inflation and energy 
7 
prices.  
8

 Should the currently assumed ROE of 9.8% be incorporated into a multi-
9 
year rate agreement? 
10 
A. 
No, in the event of a multi-year rate agreement, a premium should be 
11 
added to the updated equity cost of capital to acknowledge the risk 
12 
inherent in the multi-year commitment.

III. 
CAPITALIZATION 
1 
Q. 
What is Mr. Hale’s recommendation for the capitalization of Central 
2 
Hudson for the purpose of developing the cost of capital? 
3 
A. 
Mr. Hale recommends long-term debt ratio of 51.8%, customer deposits 
4 
ratio of 0.2% and common equity ratio of 48.0% for the Rate Year. 
5 
Q. 
How does Mr. Hale’s recommendation compare to the Panel’s Rate Year 
6 
capitalization recommendation? 
7 
A. 
The Panel recommends a capitalization with a 50.0% common equity 
8 
ratio, a long-term debt ratio of 49.8% and a customer deposits ratio of 
9 
0.2%, which is consistent with its forecasted capital structure.  
10 
Q. 
What is the basis for Mr. Hale’s recommendation? 
11 
A. 
Pages 24-25 of Mr. Hale’s testimony provide several assertions regarding 
12 
why the Company’s recommendation should be rejected in favor of his 
13 
recommendation, including: 
14 
(1) Company Witness Joshua C. Nowak’s analysis in support of a 50% 
15 
equity ratio is flawed; 
16 
(2) Central Hudson and other New York utilities have 48% equity and 
17 
maintain access to reasonably priced capital; and 
18 
(3) 50% common equity is not necessary for Central Hudson to maintain 
19 
its current bond ratings. 
20 
Q. 
Do you agree with the rationale for Mr. Hale’s recommendations? 
21 
A. 
No.  Mr. Hale’s first reason is addressed in Company Witness Nowak’s 
22 
rebuttal testimony.  The second reason reflects unsupported 
23 
PUBLIC REDACTED
982


--- Page 983 ---
Case 23-E-0418; Case 23-G-0419 
 
REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF THE FINANCE PANEL 
4 
 
generalizations that are not backed by evidence.  Mr. Hale’s third reason 
1 
(i.e., that a 50% equity ratio is not needed to support the Company’s 
2 
current bond ratings) rests on a flawed analysis that does not support Mr. 
3 
Hale’s conclusion. 
4 
Q. 
On what generalizations does Mr. Hale’s second reason rely? 
5 
A. 
Referring to Exhibit __ (ASH-11), which reflects allowed equity ratios for 
6 
New York utilities, Mr. Hale’s testimony makes the general assertion that 
7 
“all other major electric and gas utilities in New York have managed to 
8 
continue to maintain access to reasonably priced capital with a 48.0% 
9 
common equity ratio, including Central Hudson.”  Mr. Hale also 
10 
generalizes that the Company’s most recent long-term debt issuance, 
11 
which was at a higher rate than prior year debt issuances, was “more of a 
12 
function of the broad financial markets as opposed to anything specific to 
13 
Central Hudson.”  Mr. Hale offers no evidence to support his claim that 
14 
Central Hudson’s specific attributes and current circumstances did not 
15 
cause the increased debt issuance rate.  
16 
Q. 
Why do you disagree with these generalizations? 
17 
A. 
Comparison to other New York utilities is not an appropriate basis to 
18 
establish the Company’s ratemaking capitalization given recent facts and 
19 
circumstances.  In fact, Mr. Hale’s position ignores that other New York 
20 
utilities with ratemaking equity ratios of 48% were downgraded from mid-
21 
level “A”-rated companies in 2019 to predominantly “BBB”-rated 
22 
companies by the end of 2021, as is the case for Central Hudson.  A credit 
23 
PUBLIC REDACTED
983


--- Page 984 ---
Case 23-E-0418; Case 23-G-0419 
 
REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF THE FINANCE PANEL 
5 
 
downgrade resulting in further distance from an A rating is precisely what 
1 
Central Hudson is trying to avoid and is inconsistent with long-standing 
2 
Commission financial policies.  The Panel also disagrees with Mr. Hale’s 
3 
testimony at page 26, which claims that the Company “has not 
4 
demonstrated any reason why it is at a unique disadvantage relative to the 
5

filed its direct testimony and the release of the latest interest rate forecast 
4 
from Blue Chip Financial Forecast.  Please note that our updates continue 
5 
to reflect the Panel’s 9.8% ROE and 50% equity ratio recommendation, 
6 
and the Company’s position on cash recovery mechanisms, and therefore 
7 
does not include the impacts of a credit rating downgrade.  We estimate 
8 
the updated cost of long-term debt adjusted to be 4.50%, as shown in 
9 
Exhibit __ (FP-3R).  
10 
Q. 
How does the Panel’s updated cost of debt compare to Mr. Hale’s? 
11 
A. 
Our updated cost of debt, when aligned with Mr. Hale’s methodology that 
12 
excludes a variable rate cost update, is 4.44% which compares favorably 
13 
to the cost of debt of 4.46% from Mr. Hale’s testimony.  When all cost 
14 
elements, including variable debt rate are updated with the latest forecast, 
15 
our cost of debt is four basis points higher as illustrated in Exhibit __ (FP-
16 
3R). 
17 
Q.  
Do you agree with Mr. Hale’s position to eliminate the deferral mechanism 
18 
for the fixed rate debt? 
19 
A. 
No.  With the volatility of interest rates and continued uncertainty in the 
20 
market, it is extremely important that a deferral mechanism remain in 
21 
place.  This two-way deferral would protect customers as much as it would 
22 
protect the Company.  For example, Mr. Hale is currently including a 
23

6.28% interest rate for all future issuances in his weighted average cost of

3

4

VIII.
CONCLUSION
11 
Q.
Does the Panel have any final comments on Mr. Hale’s testimony in this
12 
case?
13 
A.
Yes.  Early in his testimony, Mr. Hale discusses the importance of using a
14 
“fair rate of return” to establish Central Hudson’s revenue requirement.
15 
On page 9 of his testimony, Mr. Hale offers the following definition:
16 
A fair rate of return for a regulated utility is one that enables the company
17 
to provide safe and adequate service to its customers, while at the same
18 
time assuring the utility continuing support in the capital markets for both
19 
its long-term debt and common equity securities at terms that are
20 
reasonable given the company’s risk.
21 
22 
Q.
Do Mr. Hale’s recommendations meet the standard of a fair rate of return?
23 
A.
No.  As the Panel has shown, Mr. Hale’s recommendations of a 9.2%
24 
ROE and 48% equity ratio: (i) do not support the Company’s current credit
25 
ratings but rather are indicative of a one notch downgrade to Baa2/BBB;
26 
PUBLIC REDACTED
1004


--- Page 1005 ---
Case 23-E-0418; Case 23-G-0419 
REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF THE FINANCE PANEL 
26 
(ii) result in a higher embedded cost of debt and average cost of capital
1 
than the Panel’s updated recommendations due to Mr. Hale’s 
2 
recommended methodology, elimination of two way deferrals and the 
3 
higher business risk associated with longer cash recoveries; (iii) are not 
4 
cost-justified for the Rate Year and ignore long-term consequences after 
5 
the Rate Year; and (iv) do not account for the higher regulatory and 
6 
business risks resulting from a number of Staff’s recommendations in its 
7 
testimony.  In our assessment, Mr. Hale’s recommendations for a lower 
8 
ROE and equity ratio will result in higher business and financial risks to 
9 
Central Hudson, which over time will translate into higher costs for 
10 
customers.  Mr. Hale’s testimony also ignores the negative implications on 
11 
the Company’s financial integrity of reduced and/or eliminated cash 
12 
recovery mechanisms and regulatory deferrals, and the higher NRAs 
13 
recommended by Staff.  Mr. Hale’s recommendations are less supportive 
14 
of access to capital markets in the face of higher risks and thus are less 
15 
supportive of the Company’s continued delivery of safe and adequate 
16 
service.  Accordingly, Mr. Hale’s recommendations fail to meet the fair rate 
17 
of return standard and should not be adopted.    
18 
Q.
Does this conclude your rebuttal testimony at this time?
19 
A.
Yes, it does.

NATURAL GAS SUPPLY REQUIREMENTS 
3 
Q.    
How does Central Hudson meet the natural gas supply requirements of its 
4 
customers? 
5 
A. 
Central Hudson meets its customers’ natural gas requirements by utilizing 
6 
various wholesale contract assets that deliver natural gas to the 
7 
Company’s four city gates.  Natural gas is purchased primarily from 
8 
suppliers located in the Northeastern United States (“U.S.”) and 
9 
transported on interstate pipelines pursuant to firm transportation (“FT”) 
10 
contracts to a Central Hudson city gate.  Natural gas is also purchased 
11 
from suppliers located in eastern Canada.  Canadian gas is transported 
12 
pursuant to FT contracts with Enbridge Gas (formerly Union Gas) and TC 
13 
Energy (formerly TransCanada) to a delivery point with Iroquois Gas 
14 
Transmission Pipeline at Waddington, New York.  The Northeastern U.S. 
15 
and Canadian supplies form a base of flowing supplies that are 
16 
supplemented with storage gas and peaking gas contracts.  Central 
17 
Hudson also utilizes short-term supply contracts to meet its customers’ 
18 
demands for natural gas throughout the year.  Offers are solicited via a 
19 
competitive Request for Proposal (“RFP”) process for the five-month 
20 
winter season (November – March) as well as monthly and/or the summer 
21 
season based on volumetric needs.  The gas supplied by the above

Q.    
How does the Company forecast its day-ahead requirements? 
4 
A. 
Central Hudson has implemented a two-model system for the daily 
5 
forecasting of natural gas requirements.  The Company utilizes a 
6 
combination of the results from an internally developed Excel spreadsheet 
7 
model and a commercially developed model, GasDay, for forecasting daily 
8 
rolling 24-hour send-out forecasts and supply requirements.  The resultant 
9 
forecast is comprised of a base load component (usage that is not 
10 
weather sensitive) and a heating usage component (weather sensitive).   
11 
Heating usage is calculated as the product of the daily forecast of effective 
12 
degree days (“EDD”) and usage per EDD.  EDD is a measurement 
13 
designed to reflect the demand for energy needed to heat a home after 
14 
taking wind and cloud cover into consideration.  A gas day (10am – 10am) 
15 
weather forecast is received two times per day from the weather 
16 
forecasting service vendor WSI, Inc.  Depending on the specific month in 
17 
the heating season, unusual weather patterns, or a particular day of the 
18 
week or weekend, minor manual adjustments to the forecasted send-out 
19 
may be necessary.  The Company has the ability to make intra-day 
20 
changes to the send-out forecast and requirements with gas suppliers or 
21 
pipelines or both, as necessary, due to changes in the weather. 
22

8

9 
service customers, who the Company has an obligation to serve.  A five

11 
Central Hudson recognizes that actions to address supply needs must be 
12 
initiated well in advance of the actual requirements, which provides the 
13 
basis and importance of the forward-looking plan.

Q.    
What does Central Hudson do with the available upstream capacity during 
1 
off-peak periods? 
2 
A. 
Central Hudson releases available upstream transportation and storage 
3 
capacity to an Asset Manager (“Manager”) under an Asset Management 
4 
Agreement (“Agreement”).  The Agreement provides the Manager with 
5 
Central Hudson’s entire portfolio of storage and transportation capacity 
6 
assets.  The Manager can utilize the Company’s excess capacity as it 
7 
sees fit to extract value after slices of the system are released to 
8 
Aggregators and the Company’s daily delivery requirements are met.  
9 
Operationally, the Company retains the responsibility to forecast system 
10 
send-out and submits supply requirements daily to the Manager, who will 
11 
transport daily base and storage requirements to the Central Hudson city 
12 
gates as necessary to assure reliable gas supplies to the Company’s full-
13 
service and delivery customers.  Further, the Agreement provides storage 
14 
refill services during the summer and, at any time necessary, the ability to 
15 
purchase or sell daily volumes of spot gas.  The Company has retained 
16 
the ability to purchase base and peaking services through a competitive 
17 
RFP process to maintain customer price transparency.  The Agreement 
18 
allows Central Hudson to optimize the value of the entire portfolio for the 
19 
entire year.  The system-wide Asset Management approach, in turn, 
20 
maximizes the Company’s ability to reduce commodity bill pressure.

Q.    
Does Central Hudson employ hedging or pricing strategies to dampen 
7

8 
A.

9 
Central Hudson’s Enterprise Risk Management Committee (“ERMC”).  
10 
Energy Resources implements the approved hedge plan through 
11 
managing physical storage injections and securing over-the-counter 
12 
(“OTC”) fixed for floating swap contracts with various counterparties prior 
13

14

15 
price of winter natural gas supply contracts.  The OTC contracts fix the 
16 
price of a portion of Central Hudson’s winter gas supply for the upcoming 
17 
heating season and dampens price volatility.  Central Hudson also refills 
18 
storage during the April – October time period to ensure that its natural 
19 
gas storage contract assets are physically full by the first of November, 
20 
prior to the start of the heating season.  The combination of financial 
21 
investments and the Company’s physical storage gas provides a hedge 
22

PROCUREMENT PANEL 
16 
 
against winter natural gas price volatility by fixing the price of Central 
1 
Hudson’s full-service customers’ natural gas usage in accordance with the 
2 
Commission’s Statement of Policy Regarding Gas Purchasing Practices, 
3 
issued and effective April 28, 1998, in Case 97-G-0600.  The hedging 
4 
strategy dampens natural gas price volatility, which translates directly to 
5 
incrementally less volatile energy bills for Central Hudson’s full-service 
6 
customers during the heating season.  Energy Resources reports on 
7 
energy procurement activities and the current status of commodity

Staff.

20 
Q.    
How does the Company currently forecast day-ahead electric energy 
21 
requirements? 
22 
1070


--- Page 1071 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____ 
 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF THE ELECTRIC AND GAS 
PROCUREMENT PANEL 
18 
 
A. 
The Company uses a cloud-based Software as a Service (“SaaS”) 
1 
application under contract with TESLA Forecasting Solutions 
2 
(“Forecasting Solutions”).  The Forecasting Solutions electric load 
3 
forecasting model uses a combination of historical hourly electric load 
4 
patterns and multiple weather forecasting services to develop a short-term 
5 
forward forecast of the expected hourly electric load.  The model produces 
6 
a forecast of hourly electric load for a seven-day period.  This hourly 
7 
electric load forecast is developed by the Forecasting Solutions software 
8 
using two different seven-day hourly weather forecasts (Maxar weather 
9 
forecast and DTN weather forecast), historical hourly electric load data, 
10 
and historical hourly weather data.  The Forecasting Solutions software 
11 
has proprietary programming routines that automatically choose the 
12 
combination of historical hourly weather data and historical hourly electric 
13 
load patterns to forecast the upcoming seven-day hourly electric load 
14 
based on the two different seven-day hourly weather forecasts.  The

Q.    
What electric generating assets does Central Hudson currently own? 
1 
A. 
Central Hudson currently owns, operates, and maintains two combustion 
2 
turbine generators (Coxsackie and South Cairo) and three small 
3

4 
Falls).  These electric generating facilities have nameplate ratings of 25.0 
5 
MVA, 25.0 MVA, 18.0 MVA, 6.0 MVA, and 3.6 MVA, respectively.   
6 
Q.    
How does Central Hudson manage these electric generation assets? 
7 
A. 
When not providing local electric reliability services, the Company 
8 
maximizes the two combustion turbine generator assets by bidding and 
9 
scheduling their availability in the NYISO Day Ahead Market and Real 
10 
Time Market for electric energy generation and ancillary services and by 
11 
using their electric capacity to financially benefit Central Hudson delivery 
12 
customers.  The three hydroelectric generating facilities are primarily run-
13 
of-river hydro units, and as such, they are used as electric load modifiers 
14 
on the Central Hudson electric system and not bid or scheduled in the 
15 
NYISO wholesale markets. 
16

18 
with FERC Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act (“PURPA”) Qualifying 
19 
Facility Independent Power Producers (“IPP”).  The aggregate maximum 
20 
generation from these 3 IPPs is approximately 11 MW.

Q.    
Does Central Hudson employ hedging or pricing strategies to reduce the 
1 
risk of market price fluctuations with respect to electric supply purchases 
2 
made for full service electric customers? 
3 
A. 
Yes, Energy Resources annually develops an Electric Hedge Plan that 
4 
recommends the volume and duration of financial and physical future 
5 
electric energy product, electric capacity product, and weather option 
6 
product needed to dampen the electric supply price volatility for full-
7 
service customers, excluding Hourly Pricing Provision (“HPP”) customers.  
8 
The annual Electric Hedge Plan is presented to, discussed with, and 
9 
approved by the Company’s ERMC.  Once approved, Energy Resources 
10 
implements the Electric Hedge Plan through competitive RFP purchases 
11 
of products including financial electric energy Contract for Differences 
12 
purchases, physical electric capacity purchases, and a winter season 
13 
financially settled weather option purchase.  Central Hudson’s goal is to 
14 
dampen the electric supply price volatility of full-service customers 
15 
(excluding HPP customers) by locking in the price of a portion of the 
16 
Company’s full-service customers’ forecasted annual electric supply in 
17 
advance of the delivery month.  Each annual Electric Hedge Plan is 
18 
developed, and the performance is measured in accordance with the 
19 
requirements outlined in the series of PSC Orders under Case 06-M-1017.  
20 
Energy Resources reviews the Electric Hedge Plan twice annually with 
21 
Staff.

III. 
LEAK MANAGEMENT 
5 
Q.    
Does Central Hudson have a gas leak management program? 
6 
A. 
Yes. 
7 
Q.    
How does Central Hudson define its leak management program? 
8 
A. 
The Company defines its leak management program as a system wide 
9 
program to identify, respond to and mitigate underground gas leaks in a 
10 
safe and cost-effective manner.  Gas leaks result from unplanned releases 
11 
of natural gas from the Company’s transmission and distribution 
12 
infrastructure.  The causes for these releases may include damage by 
13 
excavation activities or outside forces such as frost induced ground 
14 
movement, obsolete joint designs such as those associated with cast iron 
15 
gas mains, material failures and obsolete construction practices such as 
16 
the installation of bare steel gas mains and services. 
17 
Q.    
Please describe the Company’s current safety performance measures for 
18 
leak management. 
19 
A. 
The Company monitors two performance measures for leak management: 
20 
1) a Total Leak Backlog Performance Measure; and 2) Hazardous (used 
21 
interchangeably with “Repairable”) Leak Backlog Performance Measure.   
22 
1109


--- Page 1110 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____ 
 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF THE GAS SAFETY PANEL 
9 
 
Q.    
What is the Total Gas Leak Backlog Performance Measure? 
1 
A. 
The Total Gas Leak Backlog Performance Measure tracks the total 
2 
number of active leaks, including Hazardous Leaks, at Year End.  “Year 
3 
End” is defined as any time during the last ten days of the calendar year 
4 
not including any above grade leaks. 
5 
Q.    
What is the Hazardous Gas Leak Backlog Performance Measure? 
6 
A. 
Similar to the Total Gas Leak Backlog Measure, this measure tracks the 
7 
total number of Hazardous Leaks at year end.  Any above grade leaks are 
8 
excluded from the Hazardous Leaks reported at the end of the year for 
9 
this metric. 
10 
Q.    
Are all gas leaks considered ‘hazardous’? 
11 
A. 
No.  16 NYCRR Part 255 codifies which leaks are considered hazardous.   
12 
Pursuant to this regulation, all below grade leaks are assigned a 
13 
classification of Type 1, 2A, 2 or 3.  These leaks are documented, tracked, 
14 
monitored, and re-evaluated at regular intervals.  Hazardous or potentially 
15 
hazardous leaks are classified as a Type 1, 2A or 2 and have a set repair 
16 
timeframe ranging from immediate for a Type 1 classification to within 12 
17 
months for a Type 2 classification.  Type 3 leaks do not have an 
18 
associated repair timeframe and are considered to be ‘non-hazardous’ 
19 
due to the location and magnitude of below grade natural gas readings.  
20 
Type 3 leaks are re-evaluated during the next required leakage survey or 
21 
annually, whichever is sooner; to verify that the leak hazard level has not 
22 
1110


--- Page 1111 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____ 
 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF THE GAS SAFETY PANEL 
10 
 
changed.  The Company’s total leak backlog is comprised primarily of 
1 
Type 3 leaks. 
2 
Q.    
Please describe Central Hudson’s leak management program. 
3 
A. 
As leaks are identified through the Company’s inspection program, by 
4 
customers or by the public, Central Hudson investigates, classifies, 
5 
prioritizes, and schedules the repair by severity.  Typically, all hazardous 
6 
leaks are repaired until eliminated.  The repair prioritization of non-
7 
hazardous leaks is based on review of the leak parameters, as well as 
8 
experience and coordination with the Company’s LPP elimination 
9 
program.  Central Hudson utilizes both Company and contractor resources 
10 
to maintain an overall leak backlog consistent with the targets established 
11 
in Case 20-G-0429 measured at any day during the last ten days of the 
12 
year. 
13 
Q.    
Are there any factors outside the Company’s control that can impact 
14 
Central Hudson’s performance with respect to these metrics? 
15 
A. 
Yes.  External factors such as extreme cold causing ground movement or 
16 
third-party excavation practices may increase the total number of leaks 
17 
identified or found in a given year. 
18 
Q.    
Please discuss the Company’s recent performance with respect to the 
19 
leak management metrics. 
20 
A. 
Over the time period from 2018 to 2022, the Company was able to reduce 
21 
the total leak backlog from 91 leaks to 62 leaks.  Over that same period of 
22 
time, year-end Hazardous Leak totals went from six to three.  The 
23

repairing and replacing existing gas facilities.  The Company utilizes a risk 
2 
management tool known as Main Replacement Prioritization (“MRP”), 
3 
supervisory experience, and the feedback of its field crews in determining 
4 
whether a gas facility should be repaired or replaced.  If it is determined 
5 
the condition of the gas facility has deteriorated to the point where

10 
system?  
11 
A.

12

13

17

18 
flow valves to high pressure services that automatically stop the flow of 
19 
gas in the event of an excavation damage, and service valves to any 
20 
indoor meter set.  For additional details please refer to Gas Capital and 
21 
Operations Panel Testimony.

VI. 
DAMAGE PREVENTION 
3 
Q.    
What is Damage Prevention? 
4 
A. 
Damage Prevention is a programmatic action taken to increase public and 
5 
employee safety by minimizing damage to underground facilities or 
6 
infrastructure caused by mechanized excavation activities.  In the case of 
7 
the Company, this would apply to below grade electric and gas 
8 
infrastructure.  Central Hudson’s damage prevention program is based on 
9 
conformance with 16 NYCRR Part 753, guidance provided by the 
10 
Common Ground Alliance and industry best practices.   
11 
Q.    
What measures has the Company taken to improve Damage Prevention? 
12 
A. 
Central Hudson is an active member on the board of UDig NY (formally 
13 
DigSafely NY).  UDig NY operates the ‘811’ call center for upstate New 
14 
York and provides excavator training and public awareness throughout the 
15 
State in underground facility damage prevention.  Central Hudson is also 
16 
actively involved in the Hudson Valley Damage Prevention Council whose 
17 
goal is to reduce damage to below grade operator-owned facilities.  In 
18 
addition, the Company provides damage prevention public service 
19 
announcements and mailers to excavators as part of its public awareness 
20 
program to encourage calls for facility markouts and methods for 
21 
excavating safely without damage to underground infrastructure. 
22 
1120


--- Page 1121 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____ 
 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF THE GAS SAFETY PANEL 
20 
 
Q.    
Do you and your contractors participate in Certified Excavator training? 
1 
A. 
Yes.  The Company requires any internal and contractor resources 
2 
digging or any employee directly supervising employees’ digging activities 
3 
complete an initial Certified Excavator training and annual refresher.  The 
4 
initial course must be retaken every five years to keep the employee’s 
5 
certification current. 
6 
Q.    
How is the effectiveness of the Company’s Damage Prevention program 
7 
measured? 
8 
A. 
Currently, the Company tracks the number of regular, emergency and 
9 
refresh/retransmitted tickets received for the municipalities where the 
10 
Company has underground gas facilities.  In addition, the Company 
11 
investigates each notification of damage to its below grade gas facilities to 
12 
determine the root cause for the excavation damage.  Examples include 
13 
but are not limited to “no locate requests” made to the damage prevention 
14 
call center, third party negligence-digging within the tolerance zone, 
15 
mismarks due to locator error, mismarks due to lack of or incomplete 
16 
records and excavator error.  The damages by cause are normalized on a 
17 
1,000 markout tickets received basis for regular and emergency facility 
18 
locates.  These indices are monitored and reviewed monthly to provide 
19 
insight into the Company’s damage prevention performance. 
20 
1121


--- Page 1122 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____ 
 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF THE GAS SAFETY PANEL 
21 
 
Q.    
Does an underground natural gas facility have to be leaking to be 
1 
considered ‘damaged’ under 16 NYCRR Part 753? 
2 
A. 
No.  Any damage to a below grade natural gas facility that requires a 
3 
repair is considered a damage.  For example, this would include damage 
4 
to the protective coating on steel pipe even though there was no release 
5 
of natural gas. 
6 
Q.    
How are ‘Mismark’ damages defined? 
7 
A. 
‘Mismark’ damage is any damage to an underground facility that occurs as 
8 
a result of not marking or an inaccurate marking of underground facilities 
9 
due to lack of records, incorrect records, or locator error.   
10 
Q.    
You indicate that ‘lack of records’ is a cause for mismark damages.  Isn’t 
11 
Central Hudson required to maintain records of its facilities? 
12 
A.

VII. 
GAS SAFETY VIOLATIONS 
19 
Q.    
Please provide a brief description of Gas Safety Violations that are 
20 
associated with Pipeline Safety Regulations performance measures. 
21 
A. 
Each year, all Local Distribution Companies (“LDCs”) undergo an audit of 
22 
the records that document the completion of code required gas facility 
23 
1130


--- Page 1131 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____ 
 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF THE GAS SAFETY PANEL 
30 
 
inspections, as well as a field audit of construction and maintenance 
1 
activities performed by Company or Company contractor personnel.  If an 
2 
inspection or code requirement is missed, it is considered an occurrence 
3 
of a violation and noted in the audit.  The Gas Safety Violation 
4 
performance metric is intended to measure an LDC’s compliance with the 
5 
Commission’s gas safety regulations.  Multiple missed inspections under a 
6 
specific requirement of code are considered multiple occurrences of the 
7 
same code violation with each occurrence carrying a financial penalty.  
8 
The amount of the penalty is based on the risk rating of the code 
9 
requirement and the number of occurrences.  Code requirements have 
10 
been classified as “High Risk” or “Other” based on a list established by the 
11 
Commission.   
12

13 
Violations? 
14

15 
following table summarizes the violation and penalty structure.

VIII. 
GAS SAFETY ENHANCEMENTS 
1 
Q.    
What are Gas Safety Enhancement Programs? 
2 
A. 
Gas Safety Enhancement Programs are new operation, construction, 
3 
inspection, or maintenance programs that improve the safety performance 
4 
of the gas transmission and distribution system and are not currently or 
5 
formerly required to be in place by State gas safety code requirements (16 
6 
NYCRR Part 255 or 261).   
7 
Q.    
Does Central Hudson currently have Gas Safety Enhancement Programs 
8 
in place? 
9 
A. 
Yes.  Central Hudson currently has three programs in place to enhance 
10 
gas safety: a Residential Methane Detection Program, Pipeline Safety 
11 
Management System (“PSMS”), and the Community Gas Emergency 
12 
Response Drill Program.     
13 
Q.    
Please describe the Residential Methane Detection Program.. 
14

As directed in the June 14, 2018 Order Adopting Terms of Joint Proposal 
15 
and Establishing Electric and Gas Rate Plan in Case 17-G-0460, Central 
16 
Hudson developed a Residential Methane Detection Program using NRA 
17 
funds.  Two groups were targeted at the start of the program.  The first 
18 
group to be offered methane detectors were residential natural gas 
19 
customers through Central Hudson’s online “CenHub” store by receiving a 
20 
one-time credit towards the purchase of a detector.  The credit provided 
21 
the customer with a 50% savings off of the retail price of the unit.  The 
22 
second group to be offered methane detectors were natural gas 
23 
1134


--- Page 1135 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____

34 
 
customers who received Home Energy Assistance Program (“HEAP”) 
1 
assistance.  These customers were provided the opportunity to request a 
2 
free detector through the use of a postage paid opt-in card that was 
3 
included with the annual HEAP letter.   
4 
Q.    
Please describe the current status of the Residential Methane Detection 
5 
Program. 
6 
A. 
The Residential Methane Detection Program continued in the Company’s 
7 
most recent Rate Plan.  To date approximately 7,900 methane detectors

operators under jurisdiction of the US Department of Transportation.  The

goal of PSMS is to result in zero safety accidents or incidents.

3

4

5 
detail three to five years of work, participated on NGA committees to build 
6

11

12

13

11

12 
protocols and logistics of all first responder organizations within a 
13 
community.  Participants would include entities such as Gas Utilities, Fire 
14

15 
The Community Drills have been well received and continuation of the 
16

17 
included in the first years of the program.   
18 
Q.    
How have the full-scale exercises been conducted? 
19 
A. 
In June of 2022 Central Hudson hosted the first Community exercise by 
20 
simulating a third-party contractor accident that involved damage to a 
21 
section of a strip mall in the City of Kingston.  In the scenario, a backhoe 
22 
broke a building wall and damaged external natural gas facilities.  The 
23 
1137


--- Page 1138 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____ 
 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF THE GAS SAFETY PANEL 
37 
 
scenario included having injured bystanders (actors) inside of the 
1 
compromised building, it also included having news media (actors) on the 
2 
scene.  Once the drill started, all exercise participants performed the 
3 
actual steps that they would take during a real occurrence.  This included 
4 
communications within and between responding agencies.  It also 
5 
included responding to the event with the appropriate vehicles, staffing, 
6 
and personal protective equipment.  After the exercise reached the point 
7 
in the scenario where the natural gas leakage stopped and the situation 
8 
and all injured parties were safe, the 83 exercise participants, controllers, 
9 
and observers convened to discuss the response to the event during a 
10

11 
included the Company, the City of Kingston Fire Department, the City of 
12 
Kingston Police Department, and Ulster County Emergency Services (911 
13 
dispatchers).   In addition to the exercise participants, and the individuals 
14 
who assisted by helping to control the action during the event, there were 
15 
also City, County, and State organizations that sent representatives to 
16 
observe the event.  In October of 2022, Central Hudson hosted a second 
17 
Community exercise, following the same format, in the City of 
18 
Poughkeepsie using emergency responders from the Poughkeepsie area.   
19 
Q.    
Why is the Company proposing to continue this program? 
20 
A. 
Conducting these exercises will enable the Company to prepare for worst 
21 
case scenarios and for participants to learn from each other.  This will 
22 
ensure a more coordinated response when it is not an exercise.   
23 
1138


--- Page 1139 ---
Case 23-E-____; Case 23-G-____ 
 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF THE GAS SAFETY PANEL

Conducting these exercises will also ensure that first responders and 
1

Q.    
How is “year-end” defined for gas leak backlog? 
1 
A. 
In accordance with the Commission’s November 18, 2021 Order in Case 
2 
20-G-0428, “year-end” is defined as any time during the last 10 days of 
3 
the calendar year. 
4 
Q.    
What does the Staff Pipeline Safety Panel recommend with respect to leak 
5 
management targets?  
6 
A. 
Staff recommends a total leak backlog target of 49 leaks at year-end 
7 
2025.  Staff also recommends that the current negative revenue 
8 
adjustment (“NRA”) exposure of 15 basis points (“BPs”) continue, for 
9 
failure to meet a total leak backlog target of 60 or more at year-end, and 6 
10 
BPs for failure to maintain a total leak backlog target between 50 and 59 
11 
at year-end 2025.  The Company would not be subject to any penalty if it 
12 
maintained a leak backlog of 49 or less at year-end.  Staff also 
13 
recommends discontinuing the positive revenue adjustment (“PRA”) for 
14 
this metric. 
15 
Q.    
Does the Panel agree with Staff’s proposed targets and revenue 
16 
adjustments for the leak management measure?  
17 
A. 
No, the Panel does not agree with Staff’s proposed targets for leak 
18 
management for a variety of reasons.  First, Staff’s proposal appears to be 
19 
arbitrary.  While Staff purports that its targets are based on the Company’s 
20 
historical actual performance of leaks discovered, leaks repaired, and leak 
21 
backlog in the past five years (2018–2022), Staff’s proposed target 
22 
appears to actually be an arbitrary reduction to the two-year average 
23 
1146


--- Page 1147 ---
Case 23-E-0418; Case 23-G-0419 
 
REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF THE GAS SAFETY PANEL 
4 
 
(2021-2022) for this metric.  Supporting rationale for the target, however, 
1 
was not provided.  Second, the Panel does not agree with discontinuing 
2 
the PRAs associated with leak management.  Lastly, the number of leaks 
3 
found each year have not reduced in recent history, which demonstrates 
4 
that Staff’s reductions to the leak management targets are not obtainable.  
5 
Q.    
Why does the Panel disagree with Staff’s proposed total leak backlog of 
6 
49 leaks at year end 2025? 
7 
A. 
Staff does not provide a basis for the development of the leak backlog 
8 
target of 49 leaks at year-end 2025.  Instead, Staff rationalizes their target 
9 
of 49 by stating that the target is less than the Company’s two-year 
10 
average of 55 leaks.  Additionally, Staff does not provide a basis for 
11 
setting the target at a level that is six leaks below the two-year average. 
12 
Q.    
Does the Panel agree with the use of a two-year average for setting the 
13 
leak backlog target? 
14 
A. 
No.  Calculating the leak backlog of 55 leaks by utilizing only two years of 
15 
data (2021 and 2022) does not accurately reflect year-to year variability 
16 
which can be driven by several factors such as weather, material defects, 
17 
manufacture recalls, excavation damages or the number of existing leaks 
18 
removed on distribution improvement replacement projects in any given 
19 
year.  Utilizing only two years of data is not sufficient to accurately reflect 
20 
the impacts these factors may have on future leaks.

REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF THE GAS SAFETY PANEL 
5 
 
Q.    
Please describe how weather can impact the number of leaks found each 
1 
year. 
2 
A. 
Prolonged periods of colder temperatures with less snow cover drive the 
3 
frost line deeper into the ground, which in turn can cause more leaks.  The 
4 
Company generally finds more leaks in years experiencing such 
5 
conditions than in a year with a mild winter. 
6 
Q.    
Please describe the volatility in the leak backlog for the past three years. 
7 
A. 
Over the past three years, the Company’s leak backlog varied between a 
8 
maximum of 81 leaks during 2020, a minimum of 47 leaks in 2021, and 
9 
ended with 62 leaks in 2022.  The average leak backlog for this period is 
10 
63, while the standard deviation was approximately 14 leaks. 
11 
Q.    
What NRAs is the Company proposing for leak backlog? 
12 
A. 
The Company continues to propose the NRA targets and levels set forth in 
13 
the Panel’s direct testimony.  
14 
Q.    
Why is a target of 86 leaks appropriate?  
15 
A. 
A reasonable approach to setting the leak backlog target would be to use 
16 
the three-year average adjusted for volatility.  Specifically, due to the 
17 
volatility inherent in the historic year-end leak backlog, adding two 
18 
standard deviations to the three-year average would be appropriate.  
19 
Utilizing this approach would produce a leak backlog target for the 
20 
Company that is slightly greater than, but consistent with the Company’s 
21 
direct testimony target of 86.   
22

Q.    
Does the Panel concur with Staff that the replacement of LPP will have a 
1 
positive impact on Total Damages experienced by the Company as stated 
2 
on page 39 of the Staff Pipeline Safety Panel testimony?   
3 
A. 
No.  Until program completion, the Company has a much greater 
4 
exposure to damages due to associated unknown, unrecorded gas 
5 
facilities for which the Company has no records.  Replacement of these 
6 
LPP facilities requires excavation in very close proximity to other 
7 
underground facilities within urban streets.  This further increases the risk 
8 
of damaging an unknown gas facility.  Much of the pipe being replaced as 
9 
part of this program was installed in the early 1900s by individual gas 
10 
companies whose assets were assimilated into what is now the 
11 
Company’s total gas infrastructure.  Asset recording practices were 
12 
lacking at that time since minimal regulations existed and many of these 
13 
records were misplaced or lost as the gas infrastructure was passed on to 
14 
different owners.  Current recording and locating methods are extremely 
15 
robust and accurate as compared to early methods and will have a 
16 
positive impact once the program is completed.
